lessons.title: Set up your free lab
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every lab in this course runs in your own free Power Platform developer environment. You need two accounts.

  • A personal Microsoft account (Outlook or Hotmail) for your Microsoft Learn profile. Your certificates live here for life, so don't use a college email that expires.
  • A work or school account backed by Microsoft Entra ID for the free Power Apps Developer Plan. Gmail and other personal emails are not accepted.

If your college email runs on Microsoft 365, use it. If not, Microsoft's developer environment guide explains how to create a free test tenant.

The Developer Plan gives you Power Apps, Power Automate and Dataverse for learning and testing, not for production use. You can have up to three developer environments. An environment that is unused for 30 days is disabled, so sign in every week.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Before you can build anything, you need a place to build it. In Power Platform, that place is an environment. Think of it as your own private workshop. Your tools, your materials and your half-finished projects all stay inside it.

To get that workshop for free, you need the right kind of account. You also need to understand a few words Microsoft uses everywhere: account, tenant, Microsoft Entra ID and environment. This lesson explains each one, then walks you through the setup.

An everyday picture helps. A tenant is like a whole college campus. Entra ID is the campus ID-card office that knows every student and staff member. An environment is one lab room on that campus, with its own door and its own key list. Your account is your personal ID card.

Why it matters

Real companies never build and test in the same place their staff use every day. A broken test app in the live system could stop real work. So they separate work into environments, and they control who gets in with identities and licences.

You will copy that habit from day one. Every lab in this course happens in your own developer environment. You can break things, delete things and try again. Nobody else is affected.

There is a second reason. The exam does not test the sign-up steps, but it does test the ideas behind them. Questions about environments, security and who can access what all build on the words in this lesson.

How it works

1. Two accounts, two jobs. You need two separate identities.

AccountExampleUsed forWhy this one
Personal Microsoft accountAn Outlook.com or Hotmail addressYour Microsoft Learn profile, exam booking and certificatesIt belongs to you for life. A college email may stop working after you graduate.
Work or school accountAn address issued by a college or company that runs on Microsoft 365The free Power Apps Developer Plan and all the labsPower Platform needs an organisation identity in Microsoft Entra ID.

Gmail and other personal addresses cannot sign up for the Developer Plan. If your college email is not on Microsoft 365, follow Microsoft's developer environment guidance to get a test tenant instead.

2. Tenant. A tenant is an organisation's own space in Microsoft's cloud. When a college signs up for Microsoft 365, it gets one tenant. All its users, licences and services live inside it. Two tenants are fully separate, like two different campuses.

3. Microsoft Entra ID. Entra ID is Microsoft's identity service. It used to be called Azure Active Directory (Azure AD). Every tenant has one Entra ID directory. It stores the users and groups and checks passwords when people sign in. Power Platform trusts Entra ID to answer the question "who is this person?"

4. Environment. An environment is a container inside a tenant. It holds apps, flows, agents, connections and, optionally, one Dataverse database. Each environment has its own security. One tenant can hold many environments.

IdeaTenantEnvironment
What it isThe whole organisation in Microsoft's cloudA working area for Power Platform inside that organisation
How manyUsually one per organisationMany per tenant
HoldsUsers, groups, licences, all Microsoft 365 servicesApps, flows, agents, connections and a Dataverse database
SecurityWho belongs to the organisation (Entra ID)Who can make or use things in this specific area (roles)
Campus pictureThe campusOne lab room

Every tenant also has a default environment that licensed users can build in. Companies usually add others, such as development, test and production. Lesson 2.6 covers the environment types in detail.

5. Developer Plan versus trial. Microsoft offers two common free ways to try the platform.

Power Apps Developer PlanTrial
CostFreeFree
Time limitNo fixed end date while you keep using itTime-limited, then it expires unless you buy licences
PurposeLearning, building and testing for yourselfEvaluating the product before buying
Can run real business work?No, non-production onlyNo, it is for evaluation
IncludesPower Apps, Power Automate and Dataverse, including premium connectors, in a developer environmentDepends on the product being trialled

For this course, the Developer Plan is your main home. You can have up to three developer environments. Copilot Studio is licensed separately, so it may ask you to start a Copilot Studio trial. That is expected and fine.

Watch out: Microsoft disables developer environments that sit unused, and they can be deleted later. Sign in at least once a week so you don't lose your work.

6. The studios. Each product has its own website, called a studio or portal. They all open the same environment if you pick it in the environment picker at the top right.

StudioAddressWhat you do there
Power Appsmake.powerapps.comBuild canvas and model-driven apps, create Dataverse tables, manage solutions
Power Automatemake.powerautomate.comBuild cloud flows, see connectors, check run history
Copilot Studiocopilotstudio.microsoft.comBuild, test and publish AI agents
Power Platform admin centeradmin.powerplatform.microsoft.comManage environments, data policies, capacity and settings
Microsoft Learnlearn.microsoft.comStudy modules, track progress, book the exam, keep certificates

Example: Campus Help Desk

Here is how the Campus Help Desk project maps onto these ideas.

  1. Your college (or your test tenant) is the tenant. Its Entra ID knows you, your classmates and the help desk staff.
  2. You sign up for the Developer Plan with your college account. Microsoft creates a developer environment for you, for example "Asha's Developer Environment".
  3. In make.powerapps.com you pick that environment. Later, you will create the Ticket and Category tables here, in its Dataverse database.
  4. In the same environment you will build the student canvas app and the "Help Desk Staff" model-driven app.
  5. In make.powerautomate.com, still in the same environment, you will build flows that email staff when a ticket arrives.
  6. In Copilot Studio you will build the "Help Desk Assistant" agent. It must be in the same environment so it can reach the Ticket table.
  7. In the admin center you can see your environment in the list, and later look at its settings and data policies.

If everything lives in one environment, every part can find the others. If you build the app in one environment and the agent in another, they cannot see each other's data without extra work.

Common mistakes

  • Using a college email for your Learn profile. Your certificates are tied to it. Use a personal Microsoft account so they stay yours after graduation.
  • Thinking a tenant and an environment are the same thing. A tenant is the whole organisation. An environment is one working area inside it.
  • Building in the wrong environment. Each studio remembers its own choice. Always check the environment picker before you create something.
  • Treating the Developer Plan as a free production licence. It is only for learning and testing. Real users doing real work need proper licences.
  • Forgetting to sign in. Unused developer environments get disabled. A weekly visit keeps yours active.

What you should have after this lesson

  • A personal Microsoft account with a completed Microsoft Learn profile.
  • A work or school account signed up for the Power Apps Developer Plan.
  • A developer environment that you can select in Power Apps and Power Automate.
  • Copilot Studio open in the same environment, with a trial started if it asked for one.
  • Your environment visible in the Power Platform admin center.
  • A look at the exam sandbox so the question formats hold no surprises.
  • Clear answers, in your own words, to: What is a tenant? What is Entra ID? What is an environment?

domains.blurb: What each Power Platform product does and why businesses use it.

lessons.title: The Power Platform family
lessons.summaryHtml:
Power Platform is Microsoft’s low-code platform for building business solutions. Each product has one main job:

  • Power Apps builds apps: canvas apps, model-driven apps and code apps.
  • Power Automate automates processes with cloud flows and desktop flows.
  • Dataverse stores business data securely in tables with relationships and rules.
  • Connectors link apps, flows and agents to over 1,000 services such as Outlook, SharePoint, SQL Server and Salesforce. Custom connectors wrap your own APIs.
  • Power Pages builds secure websites for external users such as customers or partners.
  • Copilot Studio builds AI agents that answer questions and take actions.

The business value is speed and reach. People closest to a problem, often called citizen developers, can solve it themselves. IT keeps control through environments, security and data policies. Professional developers extend the platform with code when needed. A team mixing both is a fusion team.

Power BI handles analytics and has its own exam (PL-300). The current PL-900 outline does not test it.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power Platform is Microsoft's low-code platform. Low-code means you build software mostly by dragging, dropping and writing short formulas, instead of writing pages of code.

It is not one product. It is a family of products that share data, security and connectors. Think of a well-equipped kitchen. The oven, the fridge, the mixer and the pantry each do one job. Together, they let you cook almost any meal. In Power Platform, each product does one job, and together they solve whole business problems.

Why it matters

Most organisations have hundreds of small problems that never get fixed. A form lives on paper. An approval waits in someone's inbox. Data sits in a dozen spreadsheets. IT departments rarely have time for these jobs, because they are busy with large systems.

Power Platform lets the people closest to the problem fix it themselves. A help desk coordinator can build a ticket app in days, not months. IT still stays in control. It decides which environments exist, who can use what data and which connectors are allowed.

The business value comes down to three things:

  • Speed. Solutions are built and changed quickly.
  • Reach. More people can build, not only professional developers.
  • Control. Security, data policies and admin tools keep everything governed.

How it works

Each member of the family has one main job. Learn them as a set, because the exam often asks "which product should you use?"

ProductMain jobTypical usersKey parts
Power AppsBuild appsStaff and internal usersCanvas apps, model-driven apps, code apps
Power AutomateAutomate processesAnyone with repeated tasksCloud flows, desktop flows
DataverseStore business data securelyApps, flows and agents behind the scenesTables, columns, relationships, security roles, business rules
ConnectorsLink to other servicesApps, flows and agentsStandard, premium and custom connectors
Power PagesSecure websites for external usersCustomers, partners, the publicSites with sign-in and Dataverse data
Copilot StudioBuild AI agentsAnyone who needs a conversational helperTopics, knowledge, tools, channels

Power Apps comes in three styles. Canvas apps start from a blank screen and give you full control over layout, like designing a slide. Model-driven apps start from your Dataverse data and generate forms and views for you. Code apps are for professional developers who write web apps in code but still want Power Platform hosting, sign-in and governance.

Power Automate builds flows. A flow starts with a trigger (the event that starts it) and runs actions (the steps). Cloud flows work with online services through connectors. Desktop flows copy what a person does with mouse and keyboard on a computer, which helps with old systems that have no API.

Dataverse is the shared data layer. It stores data in tables, like a database, but adds business features such as security down to the row, relationships and auditing. Because apps, flows and agents can all use the same Dataverse tables, they all see the same data.

Connectors are ready-made bridges to other services. A connector wraps a service's API, which is the technical door that software uses to talk to it. The connector exposes friendly triggers and actions, such as "When a new email arrives" or "Create a row". There are over 1,000 of them.

  • Standard connectors cover common services such as Outlook, SharePoint and Teams.
  • Premium connectors cover services such as Dataverse, SQL Server and Salesforce, and need a premium licence.
  • Custom connectors wrap your own organisation's API so makers can use it like any other connector.

Power Pages builds secure websites for people outside your organisation, such as customers who sign in to check an order. It remains part of the family. The current PL-900 outline no longer tests how to build sites, but you should still recognise when it is the right product.

Copilot Studio builds agents: AI assistants that answer questions from knowledge sources and take actions using tools. They can be published to channels such as Teams or a website.

Around the products sit shared services. Power Fx is the Excel-like formula language used across the platform. The Power Platform admin center manages environments and data policies. Copilot, the built-in AI assistant, appears in every studio (lesson 1.2).

Who builds?

  • A citizen developer is a business user who builds solutions without being a professional developer.
  • A professional developer extends the platform with code, custom connectors or code apps.
  • A fusion team mixes both, plus IT, working on one solution together.
Remember: Power BI handles analytics and reports. It has its own exam and is not on the current PL-900 outline.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The college IT office gets requests by email, phone and walk-in. Nothing is tracked. Here is how each family member helps.

  1. Dataverse stores two tables. Ticket holds Title, Description, Priority (Low, Medium, High), Status (Open, In progress, Closed), Due date and a Category lookup. Category holds values such as "Wi-Fi" and "Printing".
  2. Power Apps canvas app: students use a simple, phone-friendly screen to submit a ticket.
  3. Power Apps model-driven app "Help Desk Staff": staff see views of open tickets, filter by priority and update status.
  4. Power Automate cloud flow: when a new High priority ticket is created, the flow posts a message in the staff Teams channel using the Teams connector.
  5. Copilot Studio agent "Help Desk Assistant": answers common questions like "How do I connect to campus Wi-Fi?" and can create a ticket if the answer does not help.
  6. Connectors tie it together: Dataverse, Outlook and Teams.

A coordinator (citizen developer) builds the apps. A developer from IT writes a custom connector to the college's student records API. Together they are a fusion team.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Dataverse is an app. Dataverse stores data. Users never "open Dataverse" to do their work; they use apps and agents built on it.
  • Using Power Apps for external customers. Power Apps is mainly for internal users. For customers or partners signing in to a website, the answer is Power Pages.
  • Confusing a connector with a flow. A connector is the bridge to a service. A flow is the automated process that uses that bridge.
  • Assuming low-code means no IT. IT still governs environments, security and data policies.
  • Expecting Power BI questions. It is part of the wider Microsoft family but not on this exam.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Which product should you use?" Match the verb. Build an app for staff points to Power Apps. Automate, approve or notify points to Power Automate. Store securely points to Dataverse. External users on a website point to Power Pages. Answer questions in conversation points to Copilot Studio.
  • Connecting to a service. "Work with SharePoint or Salesforce" points to a connector. "Our own API" or "in-house web service" points to a custom connector.
  • Old software on a computer. "No API" or "legacy desktop application" points to a desktop flow, not a cloud flow.
  • Who builds. "Business user without coding skills" means citizen developer. "Makers and professional developers together" means fusion team.

lessons.title: Generative AI across the platform
lessons.summaryHtml:
Copilot, Microsoft’s generative AI assistant, appears in every Power Platform product. You describe what you want in plain language and it drafts the result.

  • Power Apps: describe an app and Copilot creates the table and the app. Inside the studio, ask Copilot to add screens or explain formulas.
  • Power Automate: describe a flow and Copilot picks the trigger and actions.
  • Dataverse: describe your data and Copilot proposes tables, columns and relationships.
  • Power Pages: Copilot generates pages, forms and site content.
  • Copilot Studio: describe an agent and it writes its instructions.
  • AI prompts and models (in AI Hub) add AI to your apps and flows, for example summarising text or reading invoices.

The value is faster building and a lower skill barrier. The maker still reviews, tests and secures everything AI produces.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Generative AI is AI that creates new content, such as text, formulas, tables or whole apps, from a plain-language request. In Power Platform, this AI shows up as Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, and it lives inside every studio.

Think of Copilot as a very fast junior assistant. You say "draft me a ticket-tracking app" and it hands you a first version in seconds. The draft is useful, but you are still the one responsible for checking it before anyone uses it.

The instruction you give the AI is called a prompt. A clear, specific prompt gets a better draft.

Why it matters

Low-code already made building easier. Generative AI lowers the barrier again. A student who has never designed a database can describe the data in a sentence and get a proposed table. A professional maker skips repetitive setup and spends time on the hard parts.

AI also adds intelligence to what you build. A flow can summarise a long email. An app can read an invoice. An agent can answer questions from documents. These used to need data scientists. Now makers can add them with a few steps.

The catch is trust. AI can be wrong, can misunderstand the request, or can miss security needs. That is why the maker's review is part of every AI feature.

How it works

There are two different ways AI helps. Keep them apart in your head.

  • AI that helps you build. Copilot drafts apps, tables, flows, formulas and agents for you. The AI is a tool for the maker.
  • AI inside what you build. Your app, flow or agent uses AI while it runs, for example to summarise, classify or extract data. The AI serves the end user.

AI that helps you build, product by product:

WhereWhat you describeWhat Copilot produces
Plan designerA business problem, optionally with images or documentsA solution plan: roles, requirements and user stories, a process map, a Dataverse data model and suggested apps, flows and agents. You review it, then generate.
Power AppsAn app idea in a sentenceA table and a working app. Inside the studio it can add screens, write and explain Power Fx formulas.
Vibe experience in Power AppsAn app idea, in an ongoing conversationA plan, data and a working app, which you keep improving by chatting
Model-driven appsA page in natural languageA generated page (generative pages)
DataverseThe data you needProposed tables, columns and relationships
Power AutomateA process, such as "when X happens, do Y"A draft flow with a trigger and actions
Copilot StudioWhat the agent should doThe agent's name, description and instructions

AI inside what you build:

  • AI prompts are reusable instructions to a language model, with inputs and an output. Example: "Summarise this ticket description in one sentence." You call them from apps, flows and agents.
  • Prebuilt AI models handle common jobs out of the box, such as reading invoices, extracting text from images or detecting sentiment.
  • Custom models are trained on your own examples, such as your college's own form layout.
  • You find and manage these in AI Hub in the Power Apps studio.
  • Agents built in Copilot Studio use generative AI to understand questions, search knowledge and decide which tool to call.

The maker's job does not go away. After Copilot drafts something, you:

  1. Review it. Check names, data types, logic and missing pieces.
  2. Adjust it. Fix what is wrong, by asking Copilot again or editing by hand.
  3. Secure it. Set security roles, sharing and connections correctly.
  4. Test it with realistic data before real users see it.
Remember: AI output is a starting point, never the finished product. The maker stays accountable.

Copilot features depend on settings. An admin can turn some of them on or off for an environment, and availability can vary by region. If a Copilot button is missing, that is often why.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Let us use AI to start the Campus Help Desk quickly, then check its work.

  1. In Plan designer, describe the problem: "Students report IT problems by email and nothing is tracked. Staff need to prioritise and close tickets." Copilot suggests roles (Student, Help desk staff), user stories, a Ticket and Category data model, a student app, a staff app and a notification flow.
  2. Review the data model. Copilot proposed Priority as a text column. You change it to a choice column with Low, Medium and High, so staff cannot type "urgent!!!".
  3. Check that Status has Open, In progress and Closed, and that Category is a lookup to the Category table.
  4. In the canvas app, ask Copilot to "add a screen that lists my open tickets". Then ask it to explain the filter formula it wrote, for example:
Filter(Tickets, Status = 'Status (Tickets)'.Open)
  1. In Power Automate, describe: "When a ticket is created with High priority, post a message in the staff Teams channel." Review the draft, then sign in to the connections it needs and test it.
  2. Add an AI prompt that summarises long ticket descriptions into one line for staff.
  3. In Copilot Studio, describe the "Help Desk Assistant". Copilot writes its instructions. You read them and add a rule: "Never share other students' tickets."

Copilot saved hours. Your review fixed the data type, added a security rule and made sure every flow actually works.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting the draft without checking. AI can pick the wrong data type, miss a column or misread your intent.
  • Thinking Copilot publishes for you. It creates drafts. Saving, sharing and publishing remain the maker's decisions.
  • Mixing up "AI that builds" and "AI inside the solution". Copilot drafting a flow is different from a flow that calls an AI prompt at run time.
  • Writing vague prompts. "Make an app" gives a generic result. Name the data, users and goal.
  • Forgetting security. A generated app still needs the right security roles and sharing.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Describe in natural language" or "without designing it manually". The answer is usually Copilot in that product. For a whole solution from a business problem, with roles, user stories and a data model, look for Plan designer.
  • "What should the maker do next?" After any AI-generated result, the right answer is to review, adjust and test. Answers claiming AI output is final are wrong.
  • Adding intelligence at run time. "Summarise", "classify", "extract from invoices or receipts" point to AI prompts or prebuilt models in AI Hub, called from an app or flow.
  • Business value. "Faster development" and "lower skill barrier" are the benefits. "Replaces the need for review" is never correct.

domains.name: Dataverse and administration
domains.blurb: Tables, relationships, business logic, environments, security and ALM.

lessons.title: Dataverse vs a traditional database
lessons.summaryHtml:
Dataverse stores data in tables, like a database, but ships with business features built in. With a traditional database such as SQL Server you would build these yourself.

  • Security down to individual rows and columns, using security roles.
  • Relationships, business rules, auditing and search.
  • Rich column types: choices, currency, files, images, lookups and formulas.
  • A set of standard tables such as Account and Contact, based on a common data model.
  • No servers to manage: Microsoft handles storage, backups and scaling.

Compared with Excel or SharePoint lists, Dataverse is better for relational, secure and larger data. It needs a premium licence. Dataverse for Teams is a lighter version included with Microsoft Teams.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Dataverse is the place where Power Platform keeps business data. It stores data in tables, made of rows (records) and columns (fields). In that way it is like any database.

The difference is what comes in the box. Think of two ways to get a kitchen. A traditional database is an empty room with pipes and power: you buy and fit every cupboard yourself. Dataverse is a fitted kitchen: cupboards, locks, lights and labels are already installed. You can still rearrange things, but you do not start from bare walls.

A traditional database, such as SQL Server, is very powerful. But security screens, search, audit history and business rules must be designed and coded by developers. Dataverse gives these to you as settings you switch on.

Why it matters

Many teams start with an Excel file or a SharePoint list. That works for a small, simple list. Problems appear as the data grows:

  • Two people edit the same file and overwrite each other.
  • Everyone can see every row, including private information.
  • Nobody knows who changed a value, or when.
  • Data about the same thing is copied into several files and drifts apart.

Imagine a college IT team tracking student tickets in a shared spreadsheet. A student worker accidentally deletes a column. Another sees staff-only notes. The manager cannot tell which tickets were changed last week. Dataverse solves these with built-in security, relationships and auditing, without hiring a database team.

How it works

Dataverse lives inside a Power Platform environment. Each environment can have one Dataverse database. Microsoft runs the servers, storage, backups and scaling for you. You never install or patch anything.

Key built-in features:

  • Security: access is controlled with security roles. A role says what a user can create, read, update or delete, and on which rows. You can go further with column-level security to hide sensitive columns.
  • Relationships: tables link to each other, so a ticket can point to its category instead of copying the category name.
  • Business logic: business rules, formula columns and process flows can live on the table itself, so every app that uses the table follows them.
  • Auditing: Dataverse can record who changed what and when.
  • Search: fast search across tables and columns.
  • Rich data types: choice, currency, date and time, file, image, lookup, formula and more. Values are checked when saved, so a date column cannot hold the word "tomorrow".
  • Standard tables: ready-made tables such as Account, Contact and User. They follow a shared design called the Common Data Model, so apps and services agree on what "a contact" means.
  • Connectivity: the same data is used by Power Apps, Power Automate, Copilot Studio and many Microsoft services through connectors and APIs.
NeedExcel fileSharePoint listDataverse
Quick personal listGood fitGood fitMore than you need
Links between many tablesWeakBasicStrong, built in
Row and column security by roleNoLimitedYes
Business rules and audit historyNoLimitedYes
Large amounts of business dataWeakModerateDesigned for it
LicenceMicrosoft 365Microsoft 365Premium Power Platform licence

Dataverse for Teams is a lighter version built into Microsoft Teams. It lets a team build simple apps and flows inside a Teams team without a premium licence. It has fewer features and less capacity. When a solution outgrows it, it can be upgraded to full Dataverse.

Remember: Dataverse is premium. Scenarios that stress "no extra licence" often point to SharePoint or Dataverse for Teams instead.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The help desk team decides to move from a spreadsheet to Dataverse.
  2. They create a Ticket table and a Category table. Each ticket links to one category with a lookup, so "Network" is typed once, not on every row.
  3. A security role called "Student" lets students create tickets and read only their own. A "Help Desk Staff" role lets staff read and update all tickets.
  4. Column-level security hides an internal "Staff notes" column from students.
  5. Auditing is turned on, so the manager can see when a ticket's Status changed from Open to Closed, and by whom.
  6. The student canvas app, the staff model-driven app, the cloud flows and the Help Desk Assistant agent all read the same tables. There is one source of truth.

Common mistakes

  • "Dataverse is just a spreadsheet in the cloud." No. It is a relational database with security, logic and auditing built in.
  • "I must manage servers or backups." Microsoft manages the infrastructure. Admins manage environments and capacity, not servers.
  • "Dataverse is always the right answer." For a small list with no licence budget, SharePoint or Excel may be enough.
  • Confusing Dataverse for Teams with full Dataverse. The Teams version is lighter and lives inside a Teams team.
  • Rebuilding standard tables. Beginners often create their own "Customer" table when the standard Account or Contact table already fits.

How the exam asks about it

  • Choosing a data store. Clues such as "security roles", "relationships between tables", "business rules" or "auditing" point to Dataverse.
  • Cost or licensing limits. "Users only have Microsoft 365" or "no premium licences" points away from full Dataverse, toward SharePoint or Dataverse for Teams.
  • Ready-made structure. "Use existing tables for customers and contacts" or "common data model" points to standard tables.
  • Who manages what. Statements that makers must patch or back up database servers are false for Dataverse.

lessons.title: Tables, columns and relationships
lessons.summaryHtml:
A table holds rows of one kind of data. Each column has a data type: text, number, currency, date and time, yes/no, choice (a fixed list), lookup (a link to another table), file, image or formula.

Table types you should recognise:

  • Standard tables for most business data.
  • Activity tables for time-based items like emails, tasks and appointments.
  • Virtual tables that show data stored in another system without copying it.
  • Elastic tables for very large volumes of data.

Relationships connect tables:

  • One-to-many (1:N): one Category has many Tickets. The Ticket table gets a lookup column.
  • Many-to-one (N:1): the same link seen from the Ticket side.
  • Many-to-many (N:N): students take many courses and courses have many students.

Every table has a primary name column, shown whenever a row appears in a lookup.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A table holds one kind of thing, such as tickets. Each row is one ticket. Each column is one fact about it, such as its title or priority.

Think of a school filing cabinet. Each drawer is a table: one for students, one for courses. Each folder in a drawer is a row. The labels printed on every folder (name, date of birth) are the columns. A relationship is a note in a folder that says "see the Courses drawer, folder 12" instead of copying the whole course folder.

Why it matters

Good table design decides whether an app is easy or painful to build. If you store the category name as plain text on every ticket, someone will type "Netwrok", and reports will split it into two groups. If you use a lookup to a Category table, users pick from real rows and the data stays clean.

Correct data types matter too. A due date stored as text cannot be sorted by date or used in a "due this week" filter. A priority stored as a choice can drive colours, rules and flows reliably.

How it works

Table types you should recognise:

TypeWhat it is forExample
StandardMost business data. Includes built-in tables and the custom tables you create.Ticket, Account, Contact
ActivityTime-based actions that have a start, end or due date and can appear on a timeline.Email, Task, Appointment, Phone call
VirtualShows data from another system inside Dataverse without copying it.Orders kept in an external SQL database
ElasticVery large volumes of data, such as logs or sensor readings.Millions of device check-ins

Tables also have an ownership setting. User or team owned rows belong to a person or team, so security can limit users to their own rows. Organization owned rows belong to everyone, which suits reference lists.

Common column types:

  • Text (single line) and multiple lines of text for longer notes.
  • Whole number, decimal and currency for amounts.
  • Date and time or date only.
  • Yes/No for true or false values.
  • Choice: one value from a fixed list. Choices: several values from the list.
  • Lookup: a link to a row in another table.
  • File and image for attachments and pictures.
  • Formula: a value calculated with Power Fx.
  • Autonumber: an automatic ID such as a ticket number.

Every table has a primary name column. It is the text shown when a row appears in a lookup or a list, so give it meaningful values like the ticket title.

Relationships connect tables:

RelationshipMeaningWhere the link is stored
One-to-many (1:N)One Category has many Tickets.A lookup column on the "many" table (Ticket).
Many-to-one (N:1)The same link seen from the Ticket side.The same lookup column on Ticket.
Many-to-many (N:N)Students take many courses; courses have many students.A hidden linking table that Dataverse manages for you.

A 1:N relationship also has behaviour settings. They decide what happens to child rows when the parent row is deleted or reassigned. For example, deleting a parent could delete its children, or be blocked while children exist.

Remember: 1:N and N:1 are one relationship seen from two sides. The lookup column always sits on the "many" side.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create the Category table with a Name column as its primary name. Add rows: Network, Hardware, Accounts.
  2. Create the Ticket table. Title is the primary name column.
  3. Add Description as multiple lines of text, so students can explain the problem fully.
  4. Add Priority as a choice (Low, Medium, High) and Status as a choice (Open, In progress, Closed).
  5. Add Due date as a date-only column.
  6. On Ticket, add a lookup column Category pointing to Category. Dataverse creates the relationship: many-to-one from Ticket, one-to-many from Category.
  7. Later, the team wants to tag a ticket with several staff skills, and each skill applies to many tickets. That is a many-to-many relationship between Ticket and a Skill table.

Common mistakes

  • Putting the lookup on the wrong table. The lookup goes on the "many" side: Ticket, not Category.
  • Using text where a choice fits. Free text for Priority leads to "high", "HIGH" and "urgent" mixed together.
  • Using a choice where a lookup fits. If the list needs its own details or changes often, make it a table and use a lookup.
  • Thinking virtual tables copy data. They show external data in place; the data stays in the source system.
  • Ignoring the primary name column. If it holds meaningless values, every lookup shows meaningless text.

How the exam asks about it

  • Naming a relationship. Read whose point of view is used. "From the Category table" with many tickets means one-to-many.
  • Picking a column type. "Predefined list" means choice. "Link to a row in another table" means lookup. "Calculated from other columns" means formula.
  • Picking a table type. "Data must stay in the external system" means virtual. "Huge volume" means elastic. "Emails, tasks, appointments" means activity.
  • Both sides many. Clues like "each can have many of the other" point to many-to-many.

lessons.title: Forms and views
lessons.summaryHtml:
Forms show and edit one row. Views list many rows.

Form types:

  • Main: the full form for viewing and editing a row.
  • Quick create: a short form to add a row without leaving the current page.
  • Quick view: shows details from a related row inside another form.
  • Card: a compact form used in lists and on small screens.

Views choose columns, sorting and filters. Public views are shared with everyone. Personal views belong to one user. System views, such as Quick Find and Lookup, power search and lookup pop-ups.

Model-driven apps are built from these forms and views.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A form shows one row so you can read or edit it. A view shows a list of many rows.

Think of a library. The catalogue list on the screen, sorted by title, is a view. When you click one book and see its full details card, that is a form. Views help you find the right row. Forms help you work with it.

Forms and views belong to a Dataverse table. Model-driven apps are built mostly from them, so learning them means learning how model-driven apps look.

Why it matters

Different people need different screens. A manager wants a list of only the urgent, overdue items. A busy staff member wants to add a record in seconds, without losing their place. A support agent looking at a ticket wants to see the related customer's phone number without opening another page.

Forms and views let you design each of these once, on the table. Every model-driven app that uses the table can reuse them. You do not code any screens.

How it works

Form types:

Form typeWhat it doesWhen to use it
MainThe full form for viewing and editing one row. Can have tabs, sections, columns and related lists.The normal way to open and work on a record.
Quick createA short form that opens in a side pane to add a new row.Add a record fast without leaving the current page.
Quick viewA read-only block placed inside another form that shows columns from a related row.Show details of a looked-up row, such as the category's owner.
CardA compact layout of a few key columns.Lists, dashboards and small screens.

A main form is organised into tabs, then sections, then columns. You can also add subgrids, which list related rows inside the form. You edit forms in the form designer by dragging columns onto the canvas.

Views define:

  • Which columns appear in the list.
  • The sort order, such as due date ascending.
  • Filters, such as Status equals Open.
View kindWho sees itNotes
PublicAll users who can use the tableCreated by makers; one public view can be the default.
PersonalThe user who made it, plus anyone they share it withUsers create them in the app for their own needs.
SystemUsed by the platformSuch as Quick Find (search), Lookup (lookup pop-ups), Associated (related lists) and Advanced Find views.

After changing a form or a view, you must save and publish. Until you publish, users do not see the change.

Watch out: Quick create and quick view sound alike. Create adds a new row. View only displays a related row.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Open the Ticket table and edit its main form. Put Title and Description in a "Problem" section.
  2. Add a "Tracking" section with Priority, Status, Category and Due date.
  3. Create a quick create form with only Title, Priority and Category. Staff can log a walk-up request in seconds from any page.
  4. On the Category table, create a small form listing a "Team lead" column. Add it as a quick view on the Ticket main form, so staff see the lead for the ticket's category.
  5. Create a public view called "Open high-priority tickets". Filter Status = Open and Priority = High. Sort by Due date ascending. Show Title, Category and Due date.
  6. Save and publish. In the Help Desk Staff app, the new view appears in the view list and the quick create form opens from the "+" button.
  7. One staff member saves a personal view of tickets assigned to them. Only they see it unless they share it.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to publish. Saved but unpublished changes do not appear in the app.
  • Mixing up form and view. One row means form. A list of rows means view.
  • Using a main form for fast entry. The quick create form is designed for that.
  • Thinking a quick view form edits data. It is read-only and shows data from a related row.
  • Treating a personal view as company-wide. Public views are for everyone; personal views are private until shared.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Without leaving the current page" or "quickly add" points to a quick create form.
  • "Show details of the related record inside this form" points to a quick view form.
  • "List of rows filtered and sorted" points to a view. "Available to all users" means public view; "just for me" means personal view.
  • "Compact" or "on a small screen or in a list" points to a card form.

lessons.title: Business logic and Power Fx
lessons.summaryHtml:
Rules can live in several places. Pick the simplest one that works.

  • Business rules: no-code rules on a table. They can set a value, make a column required, show or hide a column, and show an error.
  • Formula columns: calculate a value with Power Fx whenever the row is read.
  • Calculated and rollup columns: older ways to compute values; rollups total related rows.
  • Business process flows: guide users through stages, such as New → Assigned → Resolved.
  • Power Automate flows: multi-step automation that reacts to events.
  • Plug-ins: C# code written by professional developers for complex server-side logic.

Power Fx is the low-code formula language used in canvas apps, formula columns, commands and more. It reads like Excel: If(Priority = "High", "Urgent", "Normal"). Try it in the console on the Lab tab.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Business logic is the set of rules your data must follow. "High-priority tickets need a description." "Email the student when a ticket closes." Power Platform gives you several places to put such rules, from no-code to full code.

Power Fx is the formula language used across Power Platform. If you have written =SUM(A1:A5) in Excel, you already know the idea. You describe what a value should be, and the platform keeps it up to date.

Think of a thermostat. You set "keep the room at 21 degrees". You do not write steps for turning the heater on and off. A formula works the same way: you state the result you want.

Why it matters

Rules that live only in people's heads get forgotten. Rules coded in one app are skipped when data comes in from another app. Placing a rule in the right tool means it runs every time, in every place it should.

Picking the simplest tool also matters. A plug-in needs a professional developer to write, test and maintain. A business rule can be built by a maker in minutes. The exam, and real teams, prefer the lowest-code option that meets the need.

How it works

Formulas vs code. Traditional code is a list of steps run in order. A Power Fx formula is a statement of a result. When the inputs change, the formula recalculates automatically, like a spreadsheet cell. In canvas apps, a few properties such as a button's OnSelect run actions in order, but most properties are plain formulas.

Power Fx basics:

  • If chooses between results: If(condition, value if true, value if false).
  • Filter returns a table of all rows that match a condition.
  • LookUp returns the first single record that matches.
  • CountRows counts the rows in a table.
  • Sum adds up a number column across a table.
  • & joins pieces of text together (concatenation).
If(Priority = "High", "Urgent", "Normal")

Filter(Tickets, Status = "Open")

LookUp(Categories, Name = "Network")

CountRows(Filter(Tickets, Priority = "High"))

Sum(Tickets, 'Hours spent')

"Ticket: " & Title & " (" & Priority & ")"

These are simplified. With real Dataverse choice columns, a choice value is written with a special name, for example 'Priority (Tickets)'.High. The formula bar suggests the right form as you type.

Records vs tables. A record is one row: a set of named values, written like { Title: "Wi-Fi down", Priority: "High" }. A table is many records. Filter gives a table; LookUp gives a record. Knowing which one you have tells you which functions you can use next.

ThisItem. In a canvas app gallery, each row is drawn from one template. Inside that template, ThisItem means "the record for this row". So a label with ThisItem.Title shows each ticket's own title.

Delegation (beginner level). When an app filters a big data source, the best approach is to ask the source, such as Dataverse, to do the filtering and send back only the matches. That is delegation. Some functions or conditions cannot be delegated. Then the app downloads only a limited number of rows (500 by default, and at most 2,000) and works on those. Results can be silently incomplete. Power Apps shows a delegation warning in the editor so you can rewrite the formula.

Watch out: A delegation warning is not an error. The app still runs, but with large data it may show wrong counts or miss rows.

Where logic can live:

ToolSkill levelWhat it doesChoose it when
Business ruleNo codeSet or clear a value, make a column required, show or hide a column, lock it, show an error. Built with a visual designer.Simple conditions on one table, such as "if High, Description is required".
Formula columnLow code (Power Fx)Calculates a value from other columns when the row is read.A derived value on the same row, such as a summary text or days until due.
Calculated columnNo code (older)Calculates a value with a condition-and-action editor.Older solutions; formula columns are now preferred for new work.
Rollup columnNo codeTotals, counts, minimums or maximums across related rows. Updated by a background job, so it can lag."Number of open tickets per category."
Business process flowNo codeShows a stage bar on a model-driven form that guides users through steps.People must follow the same stages every time.
Power Automate cloud flowLow codeMulti-step automation triggered by events or schedules, across many services.Send emails, post to Teams, update other systems, approvals.
Plug-inPro code (C#)Custom code that runs inside Dataverse when data is created, updated or deleted.Complex server-side logic no lower-code tool can handle.

Business rules can be scoped to a single form, all forms, or the whole table. With table scope, value and validation rules also run on the server, so they apply however the data is saved. Show and hide only affect forms.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Business rule: on Ticket, if Priority equals High, set Description to business required. Staff cannot save an urgent ticket without details.
  2. Formula column: add Summary with Title & " - " & Description, so views can show both at once.
  3. Rollup column: on Category, count related tickets where Status is Open. Staff see the load per category.
  4. Business process flow: stages New, Assigned, Resolved, so staff follow the same path for every ticket.
  5. Cloud flow: when Status changes to Closed, email the student.
  6. Canvas app formula: a label shows CountRows(Filter(Tickets, Status = "Open")). In the gallery, a label uses If(ThisItem.Priority = "High", "Urgent", "").
  7. No plug-in is needed. Every rule fits a lower-code tool.

Common mistakes

  • Reaching for code first. If a business rule or formula works, a plug-in is the wrong answer.
  • Confusing Filter and LookUp. Filter returns many rows; LookUp returns one record.
  • Using + to join text. Power Fx joins text with &.
  • Ignoring delegation warnings. They hide bugs that only appear once the table grows.
  • Expecting a business rule to send email. Business rules change the form and data only; messages need Power Automate.

How the exam asks about it

  • "No code" plus required, show, hide, set value or error message points to a business rule.
  • "Guide users through stages" points to a business process flow.
  • "Total or count of related rows" points to a rollup column. "Calculate from columns on the same row" points to a formula column.
  • "Send a notification", "approval" or "another system" points to Power Automate. "Complex logic written by developers in C#" points to a plug-in.
  • "Excel-like formula language" used in canvas apps and formula columns means Power Fx, not DAX or SQL.

lessons.title: Build tables with AI
lessons.summaryHtml:
You can create Dataverse tables by describing them. In Tables, start with Copilot and write something like “a table to track laptop loans with student, laptop serial number, loan date and return date”.

  • Copilot proposes tables, columns, data types, relationships and sample rows.
  • You refine by chatting: “add a column for the student’s email”.
  • You can also create a table by uploading an Excel or CSV file.

Always check names, data types and relationships before saving. AI makes reasonable guesses, not guaranteed ones.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

You can create Dataverse tables by describing them in everyday language. You type something like "a table to track laptop loans with student, laptop serial number, loan date and return date". Copilot then proposes the tables, columns and data types for you.

Think of an architect's assistant. You describe the house you want. The assistant sketches a floor plan. You still walk through it, move a wall, and approve it before building starts. Copilot sketches the data design; you check and approve it.

Why it matters

Designing tables is a hard first step for beginners. You must guess the right columns, pick data types and decide how tables link. Mistakes here spread into every app and flow built later.

AI speeds up the first draft. A student club officer, for example, can go from an idea to working tables in minutes, with sample rows to test with. That leaves more time for the important part: checking that the design really fits the business.

How it works

There are several ways to create a Dataverse table:

MethodHow it worksBest when
Describe it to CopilotWrite a description; Copilot proposes tables, columns, types, relationships and sample rows.You know the idea but not the exact design.
Import from a fileUpload an Excel or CSV file; the columns and rows become a table. Copilot can help name columns and pick types.The data already exists in a spreadsheet.
Create manuallyName the table and add each column yourself.You need full control, or the design is already decided.
Plan designerDescribe a whole business problem. Copilot drafts a solution plan, including a Dataverse data model and suggested apps, flows and agents.You are designing a complete solution, not a single table.

The Copilot flow for tables usually goes like this:

  1. In Power Apps, open Tables and choose to start with Copilot.
  2. Describe what you need to track. Name the key facts, and mention links to other tables.
  3. Copilot proposes one or more tables, their columns, data types and relationships. It can also add sample data so you can test right away.
  4. Refine by chatting: "add a column for the student's email", "make the rating a whole number". You can also edit the proposal directly.
  5. Review everything, then save. The tables are created in your environment like any other table.

What to check before saving:

  • Names: are table and column names clear and consistent?
  • Data types: dates as date, amounts as currency or number, fixed lists as choice.
  • Relationships: does a link to another table use a lookup, not plain text?
  • Existing tables: should you reuse a standard or existing table instead of a new copy?
  • Primary name column: will its values make sense in lookups?
Remember: AI output is a draft. Copilot makes reasonable guesses, not guaranteed ones. The maker is responsible for the final design.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The team wants to collect student feedback on closed tickets.
  2. In Tables, a maker starts with Copilot and writes: "A table to record student feedback on help desk tickets with a rating from 1 to 5, comments and a link to the ticket."
  3. Copilot proposes a Feedback table with Rating, Comments and a Ticket column, plus a few sample rows.
  4. The maker asks: "Add a column for the date of the feedback." Copilot adds a date column.
  5. Review finds two problems. Rating was proposed as text; the maker changes it to whole number. The Ticket column is checked to make sure it is a lookup to the existing Ticket table, not a new table or a text field.
  6. The maker saves the table and adds two real rows to test.
  7. Now the canvas app can show a feedback screen, and a cloud flow can ask for feedback when a ticket closes.

Common mistakes

  • Saving without review. AI can pick the wrong type, such as text for a number or a date.
  • Accepting duplicate tables. Copilot may create a new "Ticket" table when you already have one. Link to the existing table instead.
  • Vague prompts. "A table for feedback" gives a weak draft. Naming the facts and links gives a much better one.
  • Thinking SQL commands are used. Makers do not write SQL to create tables in the maker portal.
  • Keeping sample data in production. Sample rows are for testing; remove them before real users arrive.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Describe in natural language" or "without designing columns manually" points to creating tables with Copilot.
  • "Data already in a spreadsheet" points to creating a table from an Excel or CSV file.
  • "Copilot generated the tables; what next?" The answer is to review and adjust names, types and relationships, not to save or share straight away.
  • "Describe a whole business problem" with roles, processes and apps points to Plan designer rather than a single table.

lessons.title: Environments
lessons.summaryHtml:
An environment is a container for apps, flows, agents and data. Each has its own security, region and, optionally, a Dataverse database. Admins manage them in the Power Platform admin center.

  • Default: created automatically for every tenant. Everyone can build there, so avoid it for serious work.
  • Production: for solutions people use every day.
  • Sandbox: for testing. It can be reset or copied.
  • Trial: short-term, expires after 30 days.
  • Developer: a personal environment for one maker.
  • Dataverse for Teams: created when a team builds with Teams.

Good practice is separate environments for development, test and production. Managed Environments add extra governance features such as usage insights and sharing limits.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An environment is a separate space where you build and store Power Platform work. It holds apps, flows, agents, connections and, if you add one, a Dataverse database.

Think of a college building with several rooms. One room is a practice lab where students can break things. Another is the exam hall, where everything must work and nobody experiments. Each room has its own key, its own furniture and its own rules. Environments are those rooms.

Things in one environment do not appear in another. An app you build in your development environment is invisible in production until you move it there on purpose.

Why it matters

Imagine the college IT team edits the live help desk app during exam week. A small mistake breaks the ticket form. Hundreds of students cannot report problems. Staff lose a day of work.

Environments prevent this. Makers change things in a development space. Testers check the changes in a test space. Only approved work reaches production, where real users work every day.

Environments also solve other business problems:

  • Data location. Each environment lives in a region, such as Europe or India. Some laws require data to stay in a country or area.
  • Separation of teams. Finance and the help desk can have their own environments, so one team cannot see or change the other’s data.
  • Different rules. Admins can apply stricter policies to production than to a practice space.

How it works

Admins create and manage environments in the Power Platform admin center. Each environment has a few key settings:

  • Type: what the environment is for (see the table below).
  • Region: where the data is stored. You choose it when you create the environment.
  • Dataverse: an environment can have one Dataverse database or none. You can add Dataverse later if you did not add it at first.
  • Security group: an optional Microsoft Entra ID group. Only its members can be added to the environment. This is a simple way to control who gets in.
  • Security roles: inside the environment, roles decide what each person can do (Lesson 2.7).

These are the environment types you need to know:

TypeWhat it is forKey facts
DefaultPersonal productivity and quick experimentsCreated automatically for every tenant. Every licensed user can build there. You cannot delete it. Avoid it for important business solutions.
ProductionSolutions people rely on every dayIntended for live, permanent work. Treat changes with care.
SandboxDevelopment and testingCan be reset, copied and restored. Good for trying changes safely before production.
TrialShort-term evaluationExpires after 30 days.
DeveloperOne maker learning or buildingA personal environment. Only its owner uses it.
Dataverse for TeamsSimple apps built inside Microsoft TeamsCreated automatically when a team first builds an app or agent in Teams. Uses a lighter version of Dataverse.

The environment strategy. Good practice is to use at least three environments for important work:

  1. Development (often a sandbox or developer environment): makers build here.
  2. Test (a sandbox): testers check the work with sample data.
  3. Production: real users work here.

Work moves between them in a solution (Lesson 2.10). You never copy apps by hand.

Managed Environments. This is a set of premium governance features an admin can switch on for an environment. It does not change the environment type. Examples include:

  • Usage insights and a weekly digest email for admins.
  • Limits on sharing, such as stopping makers from sharing an app with everyone.
  • Rules that check solutions for quality before import.
  • Extra controls that help keep production tidy and safe.
Remember: the environment is the container. The region decides where data lives. The security group decides who can get in. Security roles decide what people can do once inside.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The college IT team plans environments for the help desk project.

  1. They do not build in the Default environment, because every student maker can create things there.
  2. They create a sandbox called “Help Desk Dev” in their own region and add Dataverse. Makers build the Ticket and Category tables, the student canvas app, the “Help Desk Staff” model-driven app, the flows and the “Help Desk Assistant” agent here.
  3. They create a second sandbox called “Help Desk Test”. A few staff try the apps with fake tickets. If testing makes a mess, the admin resets it.
  4. They create a production environment called “Help Desk”. They link it to an Entra ID security group containing IT staff and students, so outsiders cannot be added.
  5. They turn on Managed Environments for production. They limit sharing and read the weekly digest to see which apps are used.
  6. Each change moves Dev to Test to Production inside a solution. In the lab you create a developer environment called “Help Desk Test” to practise the same idea.

Common mistakes

  • Building business apps in Default. It is shared by everyone and hard to govern. Use a dedicated environment.
  • Thinking environments share data. Each environment has its own Dataverse database. A table in Dev is not in Production until you deploy it.
  • Confusing a sandbox with a trial. A trial expires after 30 days. A sandbox does not expire and is meant for ongoing testing.
  • Thinking Managed Environments is an environment type. It is a set of features you switch on for an existing environment.
  • Forgetting region. You pick the region when you create the environment, so plan it with data rules in mind.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Test changes safely”, “reset”, “copy”, “before production” point to a sandbox.
  • “Data must stay in a country or area” points to the environment’s region.
  • “Only members of a group can access the environment” points to a security group on the environment.
  • “Usage insights”, “limit sharing”, “weekly digest”, “extra governance” point to Managed Environments.

lessons.title: The security model
lessons.summaryHtml:
Security works in layers:

  1. Microsoft Entra ID signs the user in.
  2. The user needs a licence and access to the environment (often controlled by a security group).
  3. Security roles grant privileges on each table: create, read, write, delete, append, append to, assign and share.
  4. Each privilege has an access level: user (own rows), business unit, parent-child business units, or organization (all rows).
  5. Column security protects sensitive columns, and rows can be shared with specific people or teams.

Business units and teams group users for security. Common roles: System Administrator (everything), System Customizer (change the schema), Environment Maker (build apps and flows) and Basic User (use apps).

Sharing an app does not give access to its data. Users also need a security role with the right table privileges.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Security in Power Platform decides who can get in and what they can do with the data. It works in layers, like the checks at an airport.

First you show your ID at the door. Then your ticket must be valid for this flight. Then your boarding pass decides which seat you sit in. A person must pass every check. Failing any one of them stops them.

In Power Platform the ID check is Microsoft Entra ID. The later checks are licences, environment access, security roles and finer controls on rows and columns.

Why it matters

A help desk holds personal information. A student may describe a health problem or a disciplinary issue in a ticket. Other students must never see it.

At the same time, staff must see every ticket so they can help. A manager may need reports across all departments. One app, one table, but very different rights for different people.

The security model lets you give each person exactly the access they need. This is called least privilege: give the minimum rights needed to do the job.

How it works

Dataverse security is built from a few parts:

  • Business units: groups that mirror the organisation’s structure, such as departments. Every environment has one root business unit. Each user belongs to one business unit.
  • Teams: groups of users. You can give a team a security role, and all members get it. A team can also be linked to an Entra ID group.
  • Security roles: a set of privileges on each table, each with an access level.
  • Ownership: most rows are owned by a user or a team. Access levels use ownership to decide which rows you can reach.

The eight table privileges. A security role sets these for every table:

PrivilegeWhat it allowsHelp desk example
CreateAdd new rowsA student logs a new ticket.
ReadView rowsA student opens their ticket list.
WriteChange existing rowsStaff change a ticket’s Status to In progress.
DeleteRemove rowsAn admin deletes a duplicate ticket.
AppendLink this row to another rowSetting a ticket’s Category lookup needs Append on Ticket.
Append ToLet other rows be linked to this rowThat same lookup needs Append To on Category.
AssignGive ownership of a row to someone elseA supervisor assigns a ticket to a technician.
ShareGive another person access to one specific rowA technician shares one ticket with a colleague for advice.

Access levels. Each privilege also has a level. The level says how many rows the privilege covers:

Access levelRows coveredTypical use
NoneNo rowsThe person must not use this table at all.
UserRows the user owns, plus rows shared with them or owned by their teamsStudents see only their own tickets.
Business UnitAll rows in the user’s own business unitLibrary staff see all library tickets.
Parent: Child Business UnitsRows in the user’s business unit and all units below itA head of IT sees tickets for IT and its sub-departments.
OrganizationAll rows in the environmentEveryone can read the Category list.

Common built-in roles:

  • System Administrator: full rights over everything in the environment.
  • System Customizer: can change the data model (tables, columns, forms) but is not a full admin over all data.
  • Environment Maker: can create apps, flows and other resources, but gets no special access to data.
  • Basic User: can run apps and work with common tables. Often copied as a starting point for custom roles.

Roles add together. If a person has two roles, they get the most generous combination of both.

How a request is authorised, layer by layer. Say a student opens the canvas app and asks to read a ticket. The platform checks in order:

  1. Authentication (Entra ID). Is this a real, signed-in user in the tenant? If not, stop.
  2. Licence. Does the user have a licence that covers this app and its data? If not, stop.
  3. Environment access. Is the user a member of the environment’s security group, if one is set, and a user in the environment? If not, stop.
  4. App access. Has the app been shared with the user? Sharing lets them open the app. It does not give data.
  5. Security role privilege. Do the user’s roles (direct or through a team) include Read on Ticket? If not, stop.
  6. Access level and ownership. Is this row within the level? With User level, the student must own the row, or it must be shared with them or their team.
  7. Record sharing. If the level does not cover the row, a direct share can still grant access to that one row.
  8. Column security. Even with the row, a protected column stays hidden unless a column security profile allows it.
Watch out: sharing an app is not the same as giving data access. Users need a security role with the right table privileges too.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The admin copies Basic User and names it Help Desk Student.
  2. On Ticket, they give Create, Read and Write at User level, and Append at User level. Students see and edit only their own tickets.
  3. On Category, they give Read and Append To at Organization level. Every student sees the full category list and can pick one.
  4. They create a Help Desk Technician role with Read, Write and Assign on Ticket at Business Unit level for the IT department.
  5. The IT manager gets a role with Read at Parent: Child Business Units, covering IT and its sub-teams.
  6. They add a hidden “Internal notes” column and protect it with column security. Only technicians have a profile that can read it.
  7. They give the student role to an Entra ID group team, so new students get access when IT adds them to the group.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking sharing an app shares its data. It only lets people open the app.
  • Mixing up Append and Append To. Append is on the row that holds the lookup. Append To is on the row being pointed to.
  • Using Organization level for everything. It is easy, but breaks least privilege.
  • Thinking Environment Maker can see all data. It lets you build, not read every row.
  • Using a whole security role to hide one column. For a single sensitive column, use column security.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Only their own records” points to the User access level. “Everyone in the department” points to Business Unit. “All records” points to Organization.
  • “Create apps and flows but not admin” points to Environment Maker. “Change tables and forms” points to System Customizer.
  • “Hide salary” or “protect one field” points to column security.
  • “App shared but users get data errors” points to a missing security role.

lessons.title: Privacy, accessibility and data policies
lessons.summaryHtml:
Data policies (also called DLP, data loss prevention) protect company data. Admins sort connectors into three groups:

  • Business: approved for company data.
  • Non-business: allowed, but can’t be mixed with business connectors in the same app or flow.
  • Blocked: can’t be used at all.

This stops a flow from copying Dataverse data to a personal service. Policies can apply to the whole tenant or specific environments.

Privacy: data stays in the environment’s region, is encrypted at rest and in transit, and is covered by Microsoft’s compliance certifications. Audit logs and Microsoft Purview help with compliance.

Accessibility: model-driven apps follow accessibility standards automatically. For canvas apps, use the Accessibility checker, set accessible labels, check colour contrast and tab order.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This lesson covers three ways to keep a solution safe and fair for everyone.

  • Data policies control which connectors can be used together, so company data does not leak.
  • Privacy and compliance are the protections Microsoft and your admins put around stored data.
  • Accessibility means everyone can use your app, including people who use screen readers or a keyboard only.

A data policy works like the rules at a bank counter. Staff can pass money between bank accounts. They cannot hand it to a stranger outside. Connectors are the doors, and the policy says which doors can be used together.

Why it matters

Low-code makes building easy. That is also a risk. A well-meaning maker could build a flow that copies every help desk ticket to a personal cloud drive or posts it to social media. Nobody meant harm, but private data has left the organisation.

Laws such as data protection rules expect organisations to control personal data. Accessibility laws and college policies expect digital services to work for students with disabilities. Admins and makers share this responsibility.

How it works

Data policies (DLP). DLP stands for data loss prevention. Admins create policies in the Power Platform admin center. Each policy sorts connectors into three groups:

GroupMeaningExample
BusinessApproved for company data. They can be used together.Dataverse, Office 365 Outlook, SharePoint
Non-businessAllowed, but cannot be mixed with Business connectors in one app or flow.Personal or social services
BlockedCannot be used at all.A service the organisation does not trust

Key rules to know:

  • An app or flow can use connectors from Business only, or from Non-business only. It cannot mix the two groups.
  • A policy can apply to the whole tenant, to selected environments, or to all environments except some.
  • When several policies apply, the most restrictive result wins.
  • Admins choose a default group for new connectors, so new connectors do not slip in unchecked.
  • Some core Microsoft connectors cannot be blocked, but they can be classified.
  • For some connectors, admins can go further and block individual actions or limit which endpoints can be reached.
  • Custom connectors can be classified too.

If a maker breaks a policy, they cannot save or run the app or flow, and existing ones that break a new policy can be suspended.

Privacy and compliance. Microsoft and admins protect data in several ways:

  • Data is stored in the environment’s region.
  • Data is encrypted at rest (when stored) and in transit (when moving).
  • Access is controlled by Entra ID and security roles (Lesson 2.7).
  • Dataverse auditing can record who created, changed or deleted rows.
  • Microsoft Purview gives compliance tools across Microsoft 365 and Power Platform, such as audit search.
  • Power Platform is covered by Microsoft’s compliance certifications, which help customers meet their own obligations.

Accessibility.

  • Model-driven apps are built from standard components that follow accessibility standards, so most work is done for you.
  • Canvas apps give you full control of the design, so you are responsible. Use the Accessibility checker in App checker to list issues.
  • Give each control an accessible label so screen readers can describe it.
  • Check colour contrast so text is readable. Do not show meaning by colour alone.
  • Set a sensible tab order so keyboard users move through the screen logically.
  • Add text alternatives for images and icons that carry meaning.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The admin creates a policy called Help Desk DLP for the help desk environments.
  2. Dataverse, Office 365 Outlook and Microsoft Teams go in Business. The ticket flows use these to notify staff.
  3. A personal file-sharing connector goes in Non-business. A social media connector goes in Blocked.
  4. A maker tries to build a flow that posts new tickets to social media. The designer shows a policy error, and the flow cannot be saved.
  5. The admin turns on Dataverse auditing for the Ticket table, so every status change is recorded.
  6. The maker runs the Accessibility checker on the student canvas app. It reports a Submit icon with no label and low contrast on the Priority badge. They add an accessible label, darken the colour and add the word “High” next to the red badge.

Common mistakes

  • Using a security role to stop data leaking to another service. Roles control data access. Connector rules are data policies.
  • Thinking Non-business means blocked. Non-business connectors work, just not together with Business ones.
  • Believing one tenant-wide policy is enough. Environments often need different rules, and policies can be scoped.
  • Assuming canvas apps are accessible by default. You must add labels, contrast and tab order yourself.
  • Relying on colour alone to show priority or status.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Prevent data from being sent to a personal or social service” points to a data policy.
  • “Connectors that can be used together” points to the Business group. “Must never be used” points to Blocked.
  • “Find missing labels”, “screen reader”, “contrast” points to the Accessibility checker.
  • “Record who changed data” points to auditing or Microsoft Purview.
