lessons.title: Monitoring and analytics
lessons.summaryHtml:
Makers and admins can see how solutions are used and where problems are.

  • Admin center analytics: usage of apps, flows and agents, plus capacity (database, file and log storage).
  • Managed Environments add usage insights and a weekly admin digest.
  • Monitor in Power Apps shows live events, formulas and network calls from a running app, for troubleshooting.
  • Flow run history shows each run, its inputs, outputs and failures.
  • Copilot Studio analytics show agent sessions and outcomes (Lesson 5.6).
  • Audit logs in Dataverse and Microsoft Purview record who changed what.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Monitoring means watching your solutions after they go live. Analytics means turning that activity into numbers you can understand.

Think of a car dashboard. The speedometer shows how you are driving now. The fuel gauge shows how much is left. A warning light tells you something is wrong. Power Platform has the same kind of dashboards for apps, flows, agents and storage.

Why it matters

Building an app is only the start. After launch, people ask questions:

  • Is anyone actually using the app?
  • Why did the reminder email not arrive yesterday?
  • Why is the ticket screen slow?
  • Are we running out of Dataverse storage?
  • Who changed this ticket’s priority?

Without monitoring, you guess. With it, you find the answer in minutes. Admins also use usage data to decide which apps to support, retire or improve.

How it works

Different tools answer different questions. Learn which tool fits which question.

ToolWho uses itWhat it shows
Admin center analyticsAdminsUsage of apps, flows and agents across environments
Capacity reportsAdminsDataverse storage used: database, file and log
Managed Environments insightsAdminsUsage insights and a weekly digest email
MonitorMakersLive events, formulas and network calls from a running app
Flow run historyMakersEach run of a flow, its inputs, outputs and errors
Copilot Studio analyticsAgent makersSessions, outcomes, escalations and satisfaction
Dataverse auditing and Microsoft PurviewAdmins and compliance teamsWho created, changed or deleted data, and when

Capacity. Dataverse storage is shared across the tenant and split into three kinds:

  • Database: table rows, such as tickets and categories.
  • File: attachments and images, such as a screenshot added to a ticket.
  • Log: audit records.

Admins check capacity in the admin center. Turning on auditing everywhere uses more log storage, so plan it.

Monitor. You open Monitor from a canvas or model-driven app. Then you play the app. Each action appears as an event: a formula runs, a call goes to Dataverse, a response comes back. You can see errors and slow calls. A maker can also invite a user to a monitoring session to see what happens on their device.

Flow run history. Each cloud flow keeps a history of recent runs (the lab shows 28 days). You open a run and see every step, with a green tick or a red error. Clicking a step shows its inputs and outputs. This is the first place to look when “the email never came”.

Copilot Studio analytics. These show how conversations with an agent went: how many were resolved, how many were escalated to a human, and which topics were used. You will study them in Lesson 5.6.

Auditing. Dataverse auditing records changes to rows and columns. It must be turned on for the environment and for the tables you care about. Microsoft Purview lets compliance teams search activity across services.

Remember: problem in a running app → Monitor. Problem in a flow → run history. Storage → capacity in the admin center. Who changed data → auditing.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. A student says the ticket list takes a long time to load. The maker opens the canvas app in edit mode and starts Monitor. They play the app and see one Dataverse call returning far more rows than needed. They add a filter so only the student’s own open tickets load.
  2. Staff complain that a “High priority” alert did not arrive. The maker opens the flow’s run history. One run shows a red error on the email step: the address was empty. They fix the flow so it checks for a value first.
  3. The admin opens capacity in the admin center. File storage is growing fast because students attach large screenshots. The team decides to limit attachment size.
  4. The admin reads the Managed Environments weekly digest. It shows the staff app is used daily, but an old test app has not been opened for months. They remove the old app.
  5. A ticket’s priority was changed from High to Low without explanation. The admin checks audit history on that ticket and sees who made the change and when.
  6. The agent maker checks Copilot Studio analytics for the Help Desk Assistant and sees many conversations about Wi-Fi are escalated. They plan a better Wi-Fi topic.

Common mistakes

  • Using Monitor for flows. Monitor is for apps. Flows have run history.
  • Thinking audit is always on. Admins must turn on auditing for the environment and tables.
  • Mixing up capacity and licences. Capacity is storage. Licences are rights to use a product.
  • Waiting for users to report problems. Check analytics and run history regularly.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Troubleshoot”, “slow”, “network calls”, “formulas” in a running app point to Monitor.
  • “Storage”, “database, file and log” point to capacity in the admin center.
  • “Why did the flow fail”, “inputs and outputs” point to flow run history.
  • “Who changed a record” points to auditing. “Weekly digest” points to Managed Environments.

lessons.title: ALM with Power Platform pipelines
lessons.summaryHtml:
Application lifecycle management (ALM) is how you move work safely from development to test to production.

  • Package apps, tables, flows and agents in a solution.
  • Work in an unmanaged solution in development. Deploy a managed solution to test and production, where it can’t be edited directly.
  • Environment variables and connection references hold values that change between environments, such as an email address or a site URL.
  • Pipelines in Power Platform let admins set up a deployment route once. Makers then deploy with a few clicks, with optional approvals.

Pro developer teams can also use Git integration and build tools in Azure DevOps or GitHub.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Application lifecycle management (ALM) is the process for moving your work safely from where you build it to where people use it. It covers building, testing, deploying and updating.

Think of a restaurant. The chef tries a new recipe in the test kitchen. A few staff taste it. Only then does it go on the menu. Nobody experiments on paying customers. ALM does the same for apps, flows and agents.

In Power Platform the main tools are solutions, environment variables, connection references and pipelines.

Why it matters

Without ALM, makers edit live apps directly. A mistake breaks the app for everyone. Nobody knows which version is running. Moving an app to another environment means rebuilding it by hand, and forgetting a table or a flow.

With ALM, everything travels together as one package. Production is protected from direct edits. Changes follow a clear, repeatable route with testing and approval.

How it works

Solutions. A solution is a container that packages components: tables, columns, apps, flows, agents, security roles, environment variables and more. You export a solution from one environment and import it into another.

There are two kinds:

UnmanagedManaged
Where it is usedDevelopmentTest and production
Can you edit components?Yes, freelyNo, it is locked (only allowed settings can change)
What deleting it doesRemoves only the container. The components stay.Removes the solution and its components.
How you get itCreate it in the maker portalExport a solution as managed, then import it

You always keep the unmanaged version in development as your “source”. You never edit production directly.

Solution layers (beginner view). Imagine a stack of transparent sheets on a projector. Each sheet can change how a component looks or behaves. What you see is the result of all sheets together, with the top sheet winning.

  • At the bottom is the system layer: the standard Microsoft components.
  • Above it are managed layers, one per managed solution, in the order they were installed.
  • On top is the unmanaged layer: any direct edits made in that environment.

This is why direct edits in production are dangerous. An unmanaged edit sits on top. When you later import an updated managed solution, your change is underneath and may not show. You can view a component’s layers to see which one is winning.

Publishers and prefixes. Every solution has a publisher: the person or organisation that owns it. The publisher has a short prefix. Every new component’s internal name starts with it, for example a Ticket table called chd_ticket. The prefix shows who built a component and avoids name clashes. Create your own publisher early. Otherwise a default publisher with a generated prefix is used, and names are hard to change later.

Environment variables. Some values differ between environments, such as a support email address, a SharePoint site URL or a number limit. An environment variable stores that value outside the app or flow. The variable travels in the solution. You set a different value in each environment, often when importing. Variables can hold text, numbers, yes/no, JSON, a data source or a secret kept in Azure Key Vault.

Connection references. Flows and apps use connectors, and each needs a connection signed in as someone. A connection reference is a placeholder for a connection inside the solution. When you import into a new environment, you point each reference to a connection there. Several flows can share one reference, so you update the connection once.

Pipelines in Power Platform. Pipelines automate deployment inside the product.

  1. An admin sets up the pipeline once: the development environment and the stages, such as Test then Production.
  2. A maker opens their solution and chooses to deploy to the next stage.
  3. The pipeline exports the solution as managed, checks it, and asks for environment variable values and connections.
  4. Optional approvals can hold the deployment until someone agrees.
  5. The pipeline imports the solution into the target and keeps a history of deployments.

Target environments for pipelines generally need to be Managed Environments. Professional teams can also use Git integration and build tools in Azure DevOps or GitHub for source control and automated builds.

Remember: unmanaged in development, managed in test and production. Values that change per environment go in environment variables. Connections go in connection references.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. In “Help Desk Dev”, the maker creates a publisher called Campus Help Desk with the prefix chd.
  2. They create an unmanaged solution called “Campus Help Desk” using that publisher.
  3. They add the Ticket and Category tables, the student canvas app, the “Help Desk Staff” model-driven app, the flows and the Help Desk Assistant agent.
  4. The notification flow sends email to a support address. In Dev it should go to the maker. In production it should go to the real team. They create an environment variable HelpDeskEmail and use it in the flow.
  5. The flow’s Outlook and Dataverse connections are stored as connection references.
  6. The admin has set up a pipeline: Dev to Test to Production, with approval before Production.
  7. The maker deploys to Test. The pipeline asks for the Test email value and connections, then imports a managed solution.
  8. Testers approve. The IT manager approves the Production stage, and the same managed solution is imported there with the real email value.
  9. Next month the maker adds a new column in Dev and deploys again. Production updates cleanly, because nobody edited it directly.

Common mistakes

  • Deploying unmanaged solutions to production. People can then edit production directly. Use managed.
  • Hard-coding an email or URL in a flow. Use an environment variable so each environment has its own value.
  • Building outside a solution. Components created outside a solution are easy to miss when deploying. Start in a solution.
  • Ignoring the publisher. The default prefix ends up in every component’s name.
  • Thinking deleting an unmanaged solution deletes its components. It only deletes the container.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Move apps and tables between environments” points to a solution.
  • “Locked”, “prevent changes in production” point to a managed solution. “Development”, “customise” point to unmanaged.
  • “A value that differs between test and production” points to an environment variable. “Connection differs between environments” points to a connection reference.
  • “Deploy with a few clicks”, “in-product”, “approval before production” point to pipelines.

lessons.title: Canvas apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
In a canvas app you design every screen yourself, dragging controls onto a blank canvas like a slide. Formulas are written in Power Fx.

  • Connect to many data sources in one app: Dataverse, SharePoint, Excel, SQL Server and hundreds more.
  • Common controls: gallery (scrolling list), form (view or edit a row), button, text input, dropdown.
  • Run in a browser, in Teams, or in the Power Apps mobile app.

Use canvas apps when layout matters, for task-focused or mobile apps (inspections, check-ins, expense capture), or when data comes from several sources.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A canvas app is an app where you design every screen yourself. You start with a blank area, like an empty slide in PowerPoint. Then you drag buttons, text boxes, lists and pictures onto it and place them where you want.

To make the app do things, you write short formulas in Power Fx. Power Fx is the low-code language of Power Apps. It feels a lot like Excel formulas. In Excel, a cell can say =A1+B1 and it updates by itself. In a canvas app, a control’s property can hold a formula, and it also updates by itself.

Think of it like decorating an empty room. You choose where every piece of furniture goes. That freedom is the main reason people pick canvas apps.

Why it matters

Many business tasks are small and specific. A technician needs to log a site inspection on a phone. A shop manager needs to count stock. A student needs to report a broken projector in under a minute. These jobs need a simple, focused screen, not a big back-office system.

Canvas apps solve this. A maker can build a task-focused app in hours, not months. The app can also pull data from several places at once, for example a SharePoint list and a SQL Server database. It then runs on a phone, a tablet, a browser or inside Microsoft Teams.

How it works

You build canvas apps in Power Apps Studio, the editor that opens in your browser. An app is made of a few simple parts.

  • Screens: the pages of your app. A typical app has a browse screen (a list), a detail screen (one item) and an edit screen (a form).
  • Controls: the building blocks you place on a screen. Examples: label, button, text input, dropdown, date picker, image, gallery and form.
  • Properties: settings on every control, such as colour, size, position, text and visibility. Any property can be a fixed value or a Power Fx formula.
  • Data sources: where the data lives. You add them through connectors. Common ones are Dataverse, SharePoint, Excel, SQL Server and Office 365 Users.

Galleries and forms are the two controls you use most with data.

ControlWhat it showsKey properties
GalleryA scrollable list of many rows. You design one row as a template and it repeats for every record.Items (which rows to show), OnSelect (what happens when you tap a row), Selected (the row the user picked)
Edit formOne row, with fields the user can change.DataSource (the table), Item (which row), OnSuccess (what happens after saving)
Display formOne row, read-only.DataSource, Item

Some Power Fx properties appear again and again. Learn these names:

PropertyTypeExample use
ItemsData propertyWhich records a gallery or dropdown shows
TextData propertyWhat a label shows, or what a user typed in a text input
DefaultData propertyThe starting value of an input
OnSelectBehaviour propertyWhat happens when a user taps a button or gallery row
VisibleData propertyShow or hide a control, for example with a true or false formula
OnVisibleBehaviour propertyRuns each time a screen appears

Data properties hold a formula that calculates a value and recalculates automatically. Behaviour properties (the ones starting with “On”) run actions when something happens, such as a click. Common functions include Filter, Search, LookUp, Sort, Navigate, SubmitForm and Patch.

// Gallery Items: only open tickets, newest due date first
Sort(Filter(Tickets, Status = 'Status (Tickets)'.Open), 'Due date', SortOrder.Ascending)

// Button OnSelect: save the form, then go back
SubmitForm(EditForm1); Navigate(BrowseScreen)
Watch out: with large data sources, some formulas cannot be fully run by the data source itself. Studio then shows a delegation warning, and the app may only look at the first part of the data. Use delegable functions and sources like Dataverse for big tables.

Saving, publishing and sharing. When you save, Power Apps keeps a new version. Users only see changes after you publish. Earlier versions can be restored. To give others access, you share the app with people or security groups, as a user or as a co-owner. Sharing the app does not share the data. Users also need permission to the data, for example a Dataverse security role or access to the SharePoint list.

Where apps run: in a web browser, in the Power Apps mobile app on iOS and Android, inside Microsoft Teams, and embedded in other places such as a SharePoint page. Use App checker in Studio to find formula errors and accessibility issues before publishing.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. In Power Apps, create a canvas app from data and choose the Dataverse Ticket table. Power Apps builds three screens for you: browse, detail and edit.
  2. On the browse screen, the gallery’s Items is set to the Tickets table. Each row shows Title, Priority and Status.
  3. Add a text input named SearchBox above the gallery. Change the gallery’s Items to Filter(Tickets, StartsWith(Title, SearchBox.Text)). Now the list shrinks as the student types.
  4. The gallery’s OnSelect runs Navigate(DetailScreen). The detail form’s Item is BrowseGallery1.Selected, so it shows the ticket the student tapped.
  5. On the edit screen, the Save button’s OnSelect runs SubmitForm(EditForm1). The form writes the new ticket to Dataverse.
  6. Set a label’s Text to "Hello, " & User().FullName to greet the student.
  7. Run App checker, fix one accessibility issue, save and publish.
  8. Share the app with the students’ security group. Make sure they have a security role that lets them create and read tickets.
  9. Students open the app in the Power Apps mobile app or in Teams.

Common mistakes

  • “Saving is enough.” Users see changes only after you publish.
  • “Sharing the app gives access to the data.” It does not. Data permissions are separate.
  • “Canvas apps only work with Dataverse.” They can use hundreds of connectors and mix several sources in one app. Some connectors are premium and need extra licences.
  • “Power Fx is a pro-code language like C#.” It is low-code and Excel-like, made for makers.
  • Mixing up gallery and form. A gallery lists many rows. A form shows or edits one row.

How the exam asks about it

  • Choosing the app type: clues like “custom layout”, “pixel-perfect”, “mobile”, “task-focused” or “data from SharePoint and SQL” point to a canvas app.
  • Picking a control: “show a list of records” means gallery. “View or edit a single record” means form.
  • Picking a property: “which records appear” means Items. “When a user clicks” means OnSelect. “What a label displays” means Text.
  • Sharing and running: “users cannot see my latest changes” means publish. “Run in Teams or on a phone” is supported for canvas apps.

lessons.title: Model-driven apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
A model-driven app is generated from your Dataverse data model. You choose tables, forms, views, charts, dashboards and business process flows. The layout is built for you and adapts to any screen size.

  • Data must be in Dataverse.
  • Consistent look and navigation across every table.
  • Strong for complex, process-heavy back-office work: case management, CRM, approvals.
  • Dynamics 365 apps such as Sales and Customer Service are model-driven apps.

You get less control over pixel layout than in a canvas app, but much faster building for data-heavy processes.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A model-driven app is an app that Power Apps builds for you from your data. You do not place buttons on screens. Instead, you pick the pieces: which tables, which forms, which views, which charts. Power Apps then arranges them into a finished app.

Think of a flat-pack kitchen. You choose the cupboards, the doors and the handles from a catalogue. The factory makes sure everything fits together and looks the same. You get less freedom than building from raw wood, but you finish much faster, and the result is consistent.

The “model” in model-driven is your data model in Dataverse: the tables, columns and relationships. The app is driven by that model.

Why it matters

Back-office work is often large and process-heavy. Think of a support centre handling thousands of cases, or a sales team tracking leads to deals. Staff need lists, filters, detailed forms, charts and guided steps. They need all of this to work the same way on every table.

Building that by hand, screen by screen, is slow. A model-driven app gives you it quickly. It also respects Dataverse security, so each user only sees what they are allowed to see. Microsoft’s own Dynamics 365 apps, such as Sales and Customer Service, are model-driven apps.

How it works

You build model-driven apps in the app designer. The data must live in Dataverse. The main parts are:

  • Tables: the data. Each table you add gets its own page in the app.
  • Forms: how one row is shown and edited.
  • Views: saved lists of rows, with chosen columns, filters and sort order.
  • Charts: visual summaries of a view, such as tickets by priority.
  • Dashboards: pages that combine several charts and lists in one place.
  • Site map: the navigation menu on the left. It is organised into areas, groups and subareas (the links).
  • Business process flows: a guided stage bar across the top of a form.

Forms come in several types:

Form typeWhat it doesWhen you see it
MainThe full form for a row, with tabs and sectionsOpening a record
Quick createA short form that slides in, with only key fieldsAdding a record quickly without leaving the page
Quick viewRead-only data from a related row, shown inside another formSeeing a category’s details on a ticket
CardA compact layoutSmall spaces, such as some list layouts

Views also come in types. Public (system) views are made by makers and shared with everyone who can see the table. Personal views are made by a user for themselves. There are also special system views, such as the quick find view used by the search box and the lookup view used when picking a related row.

Business process flows (BPF) guide users through the same steps every time. A BPF has stages (for example Triage, Work, Resolve). Each stage has steps, which are fields to fill in. A step can be marked required before moving to the next stage. A BPF can even move across related tables.

Responsive layout. Because Power Apps generates the layout, the app adapts to screen size by itself. The same app works on a large monitor, a tablet and a phone (in a browser or the Power Apps mobile app). You do not design separate phone screens.

Security trimming. Model-driven apps use Dataverse security. Users need a security role to open the app and to see its data. The app then hides what users cannot access. If a role gives no read access to a table, that table’s pages disappear from their navigation. If a role only allows a user to see their own rows, views show only those rows. Buttons like Delete appear only when the user is allowed to delete.

QuestionCanvas appModel-driven app
Who designs the layout?You, control by controlGenerated from components
Data sourcesMany connectors, mixedDataverse
Best forTask-focused and mobile appsComplex, process-heavy back-office work
Screen sizesYou design for themResponsive by default
Remember: you can still add custom screens to a model-driven app with custom pages (canvas-style pages) and, with AI, generative pages. The core of the app remains generated from Dataverse.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create a blank model-driven app named Help Desk Staff in the app designer.
  2. Add pages for the Ticket and Category tables. The site map now shows a “Help Desk” group with both links.
  3. Include the Ticket main form. It has a General tab with Title, Description, Priority, Status, Due date and Category.
  4. Include the quick create form so staff can add a ticket from the Category page in a few seconds.
  5. Include the view Open high-priority tickets: filter Status equals Open and Priority equals High, sorted by Due date.
  6. Add a chart of tickets by Priority, and a dashboard that shows the chart next to the open-tickets view.
  7. Add a business process flow with stages Triage, Work and Resolve. In Resolve, make a resolution note required.
  8. Give student workers a role that can read and update tickets but not delete them. When they open the app, the Delete button is hidden.
  9. Play the app on a laptop, then on a phone. The layout adapts by itself.

Common mistakes

  • “Model-driven apps can use SharePoint or Excel directly.” The app’s tables must be in Dataverse.
  • “I need to design a phone version.” The layout is responsive by default.
  • “A view and a form are the same.” A view lists many rows. A form shows one row.
  • “Sharing the app is enough.” Users need a security role that gives access to the app and its tables.
  • “A business process flow automates work in the background.” It guides a person through stages. Background automation is a job for Power Automate.

How the exam asks about it

  • Choosing the app type: “data already in Dataverse”, “complex process”, “consistent interface” and “works on any device without extra design” point to model-driven.
  • Picking a component: “navigation menu” means site map. “Charts and lists on one page” means dashboard. “Add a record without leaving the page” means quick create form.
  • Guiding users: “users must follow the same stages every time” means business process flow.
  • Security: “users should only see tables they have access to” points to security roles and security trimming.

lessons.title: Plan designer
lessons.summaryHtml:
Plan designer is an AI experience in Power Apps for going from a business problem to a working solution. You describe the problem in plain language, and can add images or documents of the current process.

Copilot then drafts a solution plan:

  • User roles and requirements (user stories).
  • A process map.
  • A Dataverse data model.
  • Suggested apps, flows and agents.

You review and edit each part, then generate the pieces. The plan is saved with the solution, so the reasoning stays documented.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Plan designer is an AI experience in Power Apps. You describe a business problem in plain language. Copilot then drafts a full solution plan: who the users are, what they need, how the process flows, what data to store, and which apps, flows and agents to build.

Think of an architect. You say, “We are a family of four, we work from home, and we want a garden.” The architect comes back with a floor plan, a list of rooms and a building schedule. You review it, ask for changes, and only then does building start. Plan designer is that architect for business solutions.

Why it matters

Many projects fail before any code is written. People start building an app without agreeing on who uses it, what data it needs, or what the process really is. The result is rework.

Plan designer makes that thinking step fast and visible. A maker, a business user or a small team can go from “we have a problem” to a structured plan in minutes. Because the plan is saved with the solution, the reasons behind each design choice stay documented for whoever maintains it later.

How it works

The process has three main phases: describe, review and generate.

  1. Describe. On the Power Apps home page, start a plan and describe the problem. Focus on the business need, not on screens. You can also attach images or documents of the current process, for example a photo of a paper form or a process description.
  2. Review the draft plan. Copilot proposes several parts. You read and edit each one.
  3. Generate. When you are happy, you ask Copilot to create the pieces. Tables, apps, flows and agents are then built inside a solution.

The draft plan contains these parts:

Plan partWhat it containsHelp Desk example
User rolesThe kinds of people who use the solutionStudent, Help desk staff, Manager
Requirements (user stories)Short needs written from a user’s view: “As a … I want … so that …”“As a student, I want to report a problem from my phone so that it gets fixed quickly.”
Process mapThe steps of the business process in orderReport, triage, work, resolve, notify
Data modelProposed Dataverse tables, columns and relationshipsTicket and Category tables, linked by a lookup
Suggested componentsApps, flows and agents that meet the requirementsA canvas app, a model-driven app, a notification flow, an agent

When you edit one part, for example by adding or changing a requirement, Copilot can update the related parts. This keeps the plan consistent.

Remember: Plan designer starts from a business problem and can suggest several components. Describing a single app on the home page starts from an app idea and builds one app.

How Plan designer compares with other AI building options:

Starting pointToolTypical result
A business problem, maybe with documents or imagesPlan designerA solution plan, then several apps, flows and agents
A description of one appCopilot on the Power Apps home pageA table and a canvas app
A conversation that keeps refining an appVibe experienceA plan, data and a working app that improves with feedback

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Open the plan experience in Power Apps.
  2. Describe the problem: “Students report IT problems. Staff triage them by priority. Students get email updates. Managers see weekly statistics.”
  3. Attach a photo of the paper form the help desk uses today.
  4. Copilot proposes three roles: Student, Help desk staff and Manager.
  5. It lists user stories, such as “As staff, I want to see high-priority tickets first.”
  6. It draws a process map: report, triage, work, resolve, notify.
  7. It proposes a data model. Compare it with your own Ticket and Category tables. Maybe it suggests an extra column, such as Location. Decide if you want it.
  8. It suggests a canvas app for students, a model-driven app for staff, a flow for email updates and an agent to answer common questions.
  9. You add a requirement: “Tickets not updated in three days are escalated.” The plan updates to include this.
  10. You review everything, then generate. The pieces are created in a solution, with the plan saved alongside.

Common mistakes

  • “Plan designer only makes one app.” It can suggest a whole solution: apps, flows, agents and a data model.
  • “It builds everything straight away.” You review and edit the plan first, then choose to generate.
  • “I must describe screens and buttons.” Describe the business problem and the people involved. Copilot works out the components.
  • “Text is the only input.” You can add images or documents of the current process.
  • “The AI’s plan is final.” The maker still owns the design. Check the data model and requirements carefully.

How the exam asks about it

  • Starting from a problem: clues like “describe a business process”, “roles and requirements” or “design a complete solution” point to Plan designer.
  • What it produces: look for the words solution plan, user stories, process map, data model and suggested apps, flows and agents.
  • Inputs: “a document or picture of the current process” is a supported input.
  • Distractors: answers like “only a report” or “a security policy” are wrong. It is a planning and building experience, not a reporting or admin tool.

lessons.title: Code apps
lessons.summaryHtml:
Code apps let professional developers write a web app in code, for example React with TypeScript in Visual Studio Code, and run it on Power Platform.

  • They use Power Platform connectors and Dataverse through generated client libraries.
  • They get the platform’s hosting, Microsoft Entra sign-in, sharing and governance, including data policies and Managed Environments.
  • Use them when a team wants full control of the user interface, or already has web development skills.

For PL-900, know when to choose each app type:

  • Canvas: low-code, designed screens.
  • Model-driven: low-code, generated from Dataverse.
  • Code apps: pro-code, fully custom, still governed by the platform.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Code apps let professional developers write a web app in normal code and run it on Power Platform. A typical setup is React with TypeScript, written in Visual Studio Code.

The developer controls every line of the user interface. At the same time, the app uses Power Platform’s connectors and Dataverse, and it is hosted, secured and governed by the platform like any other Power App.

Think of renting a unit in a managed office building. You design and furnish your own office exactly as you like. But the building gives you the front door security, the electricity, the internet and the rules everyone follows. Code apps are your own office inside the Power Platform building.

Why it matters

Some teams already have skilled web developers. They want full control of the design, or they need a very custom interface. Before code apps, they often built a separate web app. Then they had to solve hosting, sign-in, data access and security on their own. IT could not easily see or govern those apps.

Code apps close that gap. Developers keep their tools and skills. The organisation keeps one place to share, secure and govern apps. This is part of the idea of fusion teams: makers and pro developers building on the same platform.

How it works

  • Write code locally. The developer builds the app with a web framework, such as React with TypeScript, in an editor like Visual Studio Code.
  • Connect to data. The developer adds Power Platform connectors or Dataverse tables. Tools generate client libraries: ready-made code that lets the app call those data sources in a typed, simple way. The app does not need to handle connection details itself.
  • Use the Power Platform CLI. Developers use the command-line tool (pac) to set up the project and push the app to an environment.
  • Run on the platform. Once pushed, the app lives in a Power Platform environment, next to canvas and model-driven apps.

What the platform gives the app:

Platform featureWhat it means for the app
HostingNo separate web server to set up
Microsoft Entra sign-inUsers sign in with their work account
SharingShared with users and groups like other Power Apps
Data policies (DLP)Connector rules apply to code apps too
Managed EnvironmentsAdmin controls and insights cover code apps

Now the key comparison for PL-900. Learn when to choose each app type:

Canvas appModel-driven appCode app
Who builds itMakers, citizen developersMakers, often with Dataverse skillsProfessional developers
How it is builtDrag-and-drop screens plus Power Fx in Power Apps StudioChoose tables, forms, views and dashboards in the app designerWrite code (for example React + TypeScript) in an editor like VS Code
Layout controlHigh, you place every controlLow, the layout is generatedFull, you write the interface
DataMany connectors, several sources in one appDataverseConnectors and Dataverse through generated client libraries
Skill levelLow-codeLow-codePro-code
GovernancePlatform (sharing, DLP, Managed Environments)Platform, plus Dataverse securityPlatform (sharing, DLP, Managed Environments)
Best forTask-focused and mobile apps, custom screensComplex, data-heavy, process-driven workFully custom web apps by developer teams
Watch out: code apps do not escape the rules. Data policies and Managed Environments still apply. An admin may also need to allow code apps in an environment before developers can use them.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. The university’s web team wants a public-style “Help Desk Status” page for students. It must match the university brand exactly, with custom charts and animations.
  2. A developer creates a React + TypeScript project in VS Code and sets it up as a code app with the Power Platform CLI.
  3. They add the Dataverse Ticket and Category tables. Client libraries are generated, so the code can read tickets with simple typed calls.
  4. They also add the Office 365 Users connector to show the student’s name and photo.
  5. They build the interface: a status card for each of the student’s tickets and a live chart of open tickets by category.
  6. They push the app to the Help Desk environment. It appears in the app list next to the canvas app and the Help Desk Staff model-driven app.
  7. They share it with the students’ group. Students sign in with their university Entra account.
  8. The admin’s data policy blocks a social media connector. The code app cannot use it either, just like a canvas app.

Common mistakes

  • “Code apps are low-code.” They are pro-code, for developers who write code.
  • “Code apps bypass data policies.” They are governed like other Power Apps.
  • “Code apps need their own hosting and sign-in.” The platform provides hosting and Entra sign-in.
  • “Code apps cannot use connectors.” They can, through generated client libraries.
  • Confusing code apps with Power Pages. Code apps are Power Apps for signed-in organisation users. Site building with Power Pages is no longer part of PL-900.

How the exam asks about it

  • Developer clues: “React”, “TypeScript”, “Visual Studio Code”, “web developers” or “full control of the UI” plus “connectors and governance” point to code apps.
  • Governance clues: a question asking whether code apps follow data policies or Managed Environments. The answer is yes.
  • Three-way choice: “custom screens, low-code” means canvas. “Generated from Dataverse, process-heavy” means model-driven. “Written in code, still on the platform” means code app.

lessons.title: Build apps with AI
lessons.summaryHtml:
You can build every app type with AI help.

  • Canvas app: describe it on the Power Apps home page. Copilot proposes a table (or uses an existing one) and builds the app. In the studio, ask Copilot to add screens or change controls.
  • Model-driven app: start from a description or plan. Add generative pages by describing a page, and Copilot builds it.
  • Vibe experience: an AI-first way to build. You chat about what you need and Copilot builds the plan, the data and a working app, and keeps improving it as you give feedback.

In every case the maker reviews the data model, sets security and tests before sharing.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

You can now build Power Apps by describing what you want. Copilot, the AI assistant in Power Apps, turns your words into tables, screens and pages. You then improve the result by chatting or editing by hand.

Think of a helpful assistant who drafts a document for you. You tell them the topic. They hand you a first draft in seconds. You still read it, fix mistakes and decide when it is ready to send. AI app building works the same way: fast drafts, but you stay responsible.

Why it matters

Starting from a blank screen is hard, especially for beginners. Choosing columns, building screens and writing formulas takes time. AI removes much of that first effort. A business user with an idea can have a working app to test the same day.

This also helps experienced makers. They can use Copilot for repetitive tasks, such as adding a screen or writing a formula, and spend their time on the harder parts: data design, security and testing.

How it works

There are several ways to build with AI. Each fits a different starting point.

  • Canvas app from a description. On the Power Apps home page, you describe the app. Copilot proposes a Dataverse table with columns, or you can point it at existing data. You review and adjust the table, then Copilot builds a canvas app on top of it.
  • Copilot in Power Apps Studio. Inside the editor, open the Copilot pane and ask for changes, such as adding a screen or changing a control. Copilot can also help explain or write Power Fx formulas.
  • Model-driven apps and generative pages. You can start a model-driven app from a description or from a plan. Inside it, you add a generative page by describing the page you want. Copilot generates the page for you.
  • Plan designer. For a bigger business problem, Plan designer drafts a full solution plan and then generates several apps, flows and agents.
  • Vibe experience. An AI-first, conversational way to build. You chat about what you need. Copilot produces a plan, the data and a working app, and it keeps improving the app as you give feedback.
OptionYou start withAI creates
Describe an app on the home pageA sentence about one appA Dataverse table and a canvas app
Copilot in StudioAn existing canvas appNew screens, control changes, formula help
Generative pageAn existing model-driven appA new page built from your description
Plan designerA business problemA solution plan, then apps, flows and agents
Vibe experienceA conversation about your needA plan, data and a working app that keeps improving

No matter which option you use, some jobs stay with the maker:

  • Review the data model. Are the tables, columns and data types right? Is a lookup needed instead of text?
  • Set security. Who can see and change which data? Assign security roles and share carefully.
  • Test. Try normal cases and odd ones. Check accessibility.
  • Follow governance. Build in the right environment and respect data policies.
Remember: AI speeds up building. It does not take over responsibility. The maker owns correctness, security and testing.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. On the Power Apps home page, type: “An app for students to book a 15-minute slot with the help desk.”
  2. Copilot proposes a Booking table with columns such as Student name, Date, Start time and Reason.
  3. You review it. You change Reason from text to a choice column (Hardware, Software, Account). You add a lookup to Category.
  4. Copilot builds a canvas app with a list of bookings and a form to create one.
  5. In Studio, you ask Copilot: “Add a screen that lists tomorrow’s bookings.” It adds the screen with a filtered gallery.
  6. In the Help Desk Staff model-driven app, you add a generative page: “A page that summarises open tickets by category.” Copilot generates it.
  7. You try the vibe experience with the same booking idea. You chat, ask for a reminder feature, and watch the app update. You compare it with your first app.
  8. Before sharing, you check the tables, give students a role that can create and read only their own bookings, and test on a phone.

Common mistakes

  • “AI builds only screens.” Describing an app on the home page usually creates the Dataverse table too.
  • “The AI result is ready to share.” Always review data, set security and test first.
  • “AI app building works only for canvas apps.” Model-driven apps get generative pages, and Plan designer and the vibe experience build fuller solutions.
  • Mixing up Plan designer and the vibe experience. Plan designer centres on a reviewed solution plan with several components. The vibe experience is a continuous conversation that builds and refines a working app.

How the exam asks about it

  • What gets created: “describe an app on the home page” leads to a Dataverse table plus a canvas app.
  • Model-driven pages: “add a page to a model-driven app by describing it” points to generative pages.
  • Conversational building: “chat to build a complete app and keep refining it” points to the vibe experience.
  • Maker responsibility: any answer saying the maker must review, secure and test is usually right. Answers saying “nothing more is needed” are wrong.

lessons.title: Cloud flows and desktop flows
lessons.summaryHtml:
Cloud flows run in Microsoft’s cloud and connect services through connectors. There are three kinds:

  • Automated: start on an event, such as a new email or a new Dataverse row.
  • Instant: start when someone presses a button, in an app, in Teams or on mobile.
  • Scheduled: run on a timetable, such as every Monday at 8:00.

Desktop flows are robotic process automation (RPA). Built in Power Automate for desktop, they click and type in Windows apps and websites that have no API.

  • Attended: runs while a user is signed in and watching.
  • Unattended: runs on a machine with nobody signed in.

A cloud flow can call a desktop flow, so you can combine both. Business process flows are different: they guide users through stages inside model-driven apps.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power Automate lets you build flows. A flow is a list of steps that the computer runs for you, so people stop doing the same boring task by hand.

Think of a flow as a helpful assistant who follows a written checklist. The checklist starts with "when this happens" and continues with "then do this, then do that".

There are two big families of flows:

  • Cloud flows run in Microsoft’s cloud. They talk to services such as Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Dataverse through connectors. A connector is a ready-made bridge to one service.
  • Desktop flows run on a Windows computer. They copy what a person does with a mouse and keyboard: clicking buttons, typing into boxes and reading screens. This is called robotic process automation, or RPA.

A simple way to remember: a cloud flow talks to apps "behind the scenes". A desktop flow uses apps "in front of the screen", just like a person would.

Why it matters

Every organisation has repetitive work. Someone copies data from emails into a spreadsheet. Someone sends the same reminder every Friday. Someone types figures from one old system into another.

This work is slow, boring and easy to get wrong. Flows do it the same way every time, day or night.

Imagine a college finance office. Each morning a clerk exports fee payments from an old desktop accounting program and types them into a new system. The old program has no API. An API is a door that lets software talk to other software. With no API, a cloud flow cannot reach it. A desktop flow can, because it simply uses the screen like the clerk does.

Choosing the right flow type is the first design decision. It is also a very common exam topic.

How it works

Every flow starts with a trigger, the event that starts it. The trigger decides what type of cloud flow you have.

Cloud flow typeHow it startsTrigger examples
AutomatedBy itself, when an event happens in a serviceA new email arrives in Outlook; a row is added to a Dataverse table; a file is created in SharePoint; a Microsoft Forms response is submitted
InstantWhen a person starts it on purposeA button in the Power Automate mobile app; a button in a Power Apps canvas app; a selected message in Teams; a selected item in SharePoint
ScheduledOn a timetable (a "recurrence")Every day at 9:00; every Monday at 8:00; the first day of each month

Desktop flows are built in a separate Windows program called Power Automate for desktop. You can drag actions onto a canvas, or use the recorder to capture your clicks and typing. The flow can work with Windows programs, websites, Excel files, folders and more.

Cloud flowDesktop flow
Where it runsMicrosoft’s cloudA Windows computer (physical or virtual)
How it reaches systemsConnectors that use APIsThe user interface: clicks, typing, reading screens
Where you build itPower Automate in the browserPower Automate for desktop on Windows
Best forModern cloud services with connectorsLegacy apps and websites with no API
Needs a machine switched on?NoYes

Desktop flows can run in two modes:

AttendedUnattended
Is a person signed in?Yes, a user is signed in and the screen is unlockedNo one is signed in; the flow signs in by itself
Typical useHelping a worker at their desk, often started by themBack-office jobs that run overnight or in bulk
Can a person step in?Yes, the user can watch and respondNo, it must work without help
ExampleA support worker presses a button to fill a form in an old appEvery night, a virtual machine copies 500 records into a legacy system

The two families work well together. A cloud flow can call a desktop flow as one of its steps. For example, a cloud flow reacts to a new email, then asks a desktop flow to type the details into an old program. To run desktop flows from the cloud, the Windows machine is registered with Power Automate so the cloud can reach it.

Remember: business process flows are a different thing. They do not automate tasks. They show a stage bar in a model-driven app that guides people through steps, such as New, Triage, Resolve.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The help desk team wants three automations and one RPA job.

  1. Automated flow: trigger "When a row is added" to the Ticket table in Dataverse. Action: send a confirmation email to the student. Nobody presses anything; a new ticket starts it.
  2. Instant flow: a staff member presses a button called "Escalate" in the canvas app. The flow posts the ticket in a Teams channel for senior staff.
  3. Scheduled flow: every weekday at 9:00, the flow lists tickets whose Status is Open and Due date is past, and emails a summary to the team lead.
  4. Desktop flow: the campus still uses an old Windows asset register with no API. When a ticket in the Hardware category closes, a cloud flow calls a desktop flow. The desktop flow opens the asset register and types in the repair note. Because it runs at night on a virtual machine with nobody signed in, it runs unattended.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking "instant" means "fast". It means a person starts it manually. An automated flow can be just as fast.
  • Using a desktop flow when a connector exists. If the service has a connector, a cloud flow is simpler and more reliable. Screen-based automation can break when a screen layout changes.
  • Mixing up attended and unattended. Attended needs a signed-in user; unattended needs no one signed in.
  • Confusing business process flows with automation. They guide users; they do not run steps in the background.
  • Forgetting that a desktop flow needs a Windows machine that is available when it runs.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Legacy", "no API", "old desktop application", "mainframe screen" point to a desktop flow (RPA).
  • "When an email arrives", "when a record is created", "when a file is added" point to an automated cloud flow.
  • "User clicks a button", "on demand", "from a mobile device", "from a selected item" point to an instant cloud flow.
  • "Every night", "each Monday", "once a month" point to a scheduled cloud flow. Add "with no user signed in" and a desktop step, and the answer is an unattended desktop flow.

lessons.title: Common automation scenarios
lessons.summaryHtml:
Most exam scenarios use these building blocks:

  • Approvals: send approval requests people answer in Teams, Outlook or the Approvals app. Choose “everyone must approve” or “first to respond”.
  • Microsoft Teams: post messages or adaptive cards, and start flows from a message.
  • Outlook: react when an email arrives, send emails, save attachments.
  • SharePoint: react when a list item or file is created or changed; create and update items.
  • Microsoft Forms: react when a new response is submitted, then save it elsewhere.
  • Document automation: use AI to extract data from invoices and forms, and generate documents from templates.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Most real flows are built from a small set of familiar building blocks. Learn these blocks and you can design most business automations.

Think of them like LEGO bricks. An approval brick, a Teams brick, an email brick, a SharePoint brick, a Forms brick and an AI document brick. You snap them together in a flow.

Each brick is a connector, and each connector offers triggers (events that start a flow) and actions (steps the flow performs).

Why it matters

Office work is full of hand-offs. A form is filled in, someone copies it to a list, someone else emails a manager, the manager replies, and someone updates a record. Every hand-off costs time and can be forgotten.

Imagine a college events team. Students request rooms through a form. Today, a coordinator reads each response, checks with the facilities manager by email, and replies to the student. Requests get lost in inboxes. A flow can collect the response, ask the manager to approve in Teams, and reply to the student automatically. Everyone sees the same result, and nothing is forgotten.

How it works

Here are the common scenarios and what each building block does.

Building blockTypical triggerTypical actionsClue words
Approvals(Usually used as an action, not a trigger)Start and wait for an approval; create an approvalapprove, reject, sign off, manager decision
Microsoft TeamsFor a selected message; when a new channel message is addedPost a message; post an adaptive card and wait for a responsenotify the team, chat, channel
Office 365 OutlookWhen a new email arrivesSend an email; save attachments; create a calendar eventemail, inbox, attachment, meeting
SharePointWhen an item is created or modified; when a file is createdCreate item; update item; get items; create filelist, document library, file uploaded
Microsoft FormsWhen a new response is submittedGet response detailssurvey, questionnaire, form response
Document automationOften a new file or email attachmentExtract information from documents with AI; fill a document templateinvoice, receipt, scanned form, extract fields

Approvals in detail. The approval action sends a request that people can answer in Teams, in Outlook or in the Approvals area of Power Automate. You choose how the decision is made:

Approval typeWhat happensWhen to use
Approve/Reject – Everyone must approveEvery assigned person must approve. One rejection rejects the request.Decisions that need all sign-offs, such as a policy change
Approve/Reject – First to respondThe first person to answer decides for everyone.Any one manager from a group can decide
Custom responsesYou define your own answer options, such as "Repair", "Replace", "Reject".More than two possible outcomes

"Start and wait for an approval" pauses the flow until the decision arrives. Then a Condition checks the outcome and takes the Yes or No path.

Forms scenario. The Forms trigger only tells you that a response exists. You then add "Get response details" to read the actual answers. Beginners often forget this second step.

Document automation. AI models can read documents such as invoices and receipts and pull out fields like supplier, total and date. This is called document processing. Flows can also generate documents, for example by filling a Word template with data or converting a file to PDF. Together this lets you automate the full life of a document: receive, read, store, route and create.

Watch out: AI extraction is not always perfect. Good designs keep a person in the loop, for example by asking for a review when the AI is unsure.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The help desk wants students without app access to report problems through a simple form, and wants a manager to approve expensive repairs.

  1. Create a Microsoft Form called "Report an IT problem" with Title, Description and Priority questions.
  2. Flow 1 trigger: Microsoft Forms, "When a new response is submitted".
  3. Action: "Get response details" to read the Title, Description and Priority answers.
  4. Action: Dataverse "Add a new row" to the Ticket table, mapping each answer to a column. Status is set to Open.
  5. Action: Teams "Post a message" in the Help Desk channel: "New ticket: [Title]".
  6. Flow 2 trigger: a new Ticket row is added with Priority High.
  7. Action: "Start and wait for an approval" (First to respond), assigned to two IT managers.
  8. Condition: if the outcome is Approve, update the ticket Status to In progress. Otherwise, email the student that the request was declined.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting "Get response details" after the Forms trigger, so the answers are missing.
  • Picking "Everyone must approve" when the scenario says any one manager can decide.
  • Thinking approvals only work by email. People can also approve in Teams or in Power Automate.
  • Using a plain email with "reply yes or no" instead of the Approvals connector. Approvals record the decision and its history properly.
  • Assuming AI extraction is always correct and skipping human review.

How the exam asks about it

  • "A manager must approve or reject" points to the Approvals connector, usually "Start and wait for an approval".
  • "Survey", "questionnaire", "when someone submits" point to the Microsoft Forms trigger.
  • "Extract the total, date and vendor from scanned invoices" points to AI document processing.
  • "Notify the team in a channel" or "ask for input with a card" points to Teams messages or adaptive cards. "When a file is added to a library" points to a SharePoint trigger.

terms.definition: A request that one or more people approve or reject.
An interactive card posted in Teams or Outlook.

lessons.title: Triggers, actions and connectors
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every cloud flow has exactly one trigger followed by one or more actions.

  • A trigger is the event that starts the flow.
  • Actions are the steps that follow.
  • A connector packages the triggers and actions for one service.
  • A connection stores the sign-in the connector uses.

Connectors are standard (included with Microsoft 365) or premium (need a premium licence). Dataverse, SQL Server, HTTP and custom connectors are premium.

Data moves between steps as dynamic content. Expressions calculate values. Control actions add logic: Condition, Switch, Apply to each, Do until and Scope.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Every cloud flow is built from the same parts. There is one trigger at the top, then one or more actions below it.

Think of a doorbell. Pressing the bell is the trigger. Everything that happens next, like walking to the door, looking through the window and opening it, is an action.

  • A trigger is the event that starts the flow.
  • An action is a step the flow performs.
  • A connector is a package of triggers and actions for one service, such as Outlook or Dataverse.
  • A connection is the saved sign-in a connector uses to reach that service on your behalf.

Why it matters

These parts are the grammar of Power Automate. If you understand them, you can read any flow and explain what it does.

They also affect cost. Some connectors are included with Microsoft 365. Others need a premium licence. A student project that suddenly uses a premium connector may stop working for users without the right licence. Knowing the difference early saves surprises.

How it works

Triggers. A flow has exactly one trigger. If you need two different starting events, build two flows. Many triggers let you add trigger conditions or filters, so the flow only starts when it matters, for example only for High priority tickets.

Actions. Actions run in order from top to bottom. Each action can use the output of earlier steps.

Connectors. There are hundreds of connectors. They fall into groups by licence:

Standard connectorsPremium connectors
LicenceIncluded with Microsoft 365 plans that include Power AutomateNeed a premium Power Automate or Power Apps licence
ExamplesOffice 365 Outlook, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive for Business, Microsoft Forms, ApprovalsDataverse, SQL Server, HTTP, custom connectors, many third-party business systems
Typical useEveryday Microsoft 365 productivityBusiness data, databases, and calling any web API

A custom connector lets developers wrap their own API so makers can use it like any other connector. Custom connectors are premium.

Dynamic content. When you fill in an action, a panel lists the values produced by earlier steps. These values are called dynamic content. For example, after a Dataverse trigger, you can pick the ticket’s Title and drop it into an email subject. At run time, the real title replaces the placeholder.

Expressions. Sometimes you need to calculate a value, not just copy it. Expressions are small formulas written with built-in functions. They look a little like Excel formulas. Here are two simple examples:

addDays(utcNow(), 3)
concat('Ticket received: ', triggerOutputs()?['body/title'])

The first returns the date and time three days from now. You could use it to set a Due date. The second joins some text with the ticket title. The exact name inside the brackets depends on the column’s internal name, so in practice you usually pick it from dynamic content. Expressions are different from Power Fx, which is the formula language of canvas apps.

Control actions. These add logic to a flow:

ControlWhat it doesWhen to use it
ConditionChecks a rule and runs the Yes branch or the No branchTwo outcomes: is Priority equal to High?
SwitchCompares one value against several cases and runs the matching case, with a defaultMany outcomes from one value: Low, Medium or High
Apply to eachRepeats steps once for every item in a listEmail the owner of every overdue ticket
Do untilRepeats steps until a condition becomes true, within set limits on count and timeKeep checking until a status changes
ScopeGroups actions into one blockTidy a flow, or handle errors for a group of steps together

Every flow keeps a run history. You can open any past run and see each step’s inputs, outputs and any error. This is the first place to look when a flow fails.

Remember: one flow, one trigger. Actions can be many. Connections hold the sign-in, connectors hold the triggers and actions.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Goal: when a new ticket arrives, route it by priority and set a due date.

  1. Trigger: Dataverse "When a row is added, modified or deleted", change type Added, table Ticket. Dataverse is premium, so the maker needs a premium licence.
  2. Action: Dataverse "Update a row" on the same ticket. For Due date, use the expression addDays(utcNow(), 3).
  3. Control: Switch on Priority.
    • Case High: Teams "Post a message" to the senior staff channel, using the Title as dynamic content.
    • Case Medium: Outlook "Send an email" to the help desk inbox.
    • Default (Low): do nothing; the ticket waits in the queue.
  4. Save, add a High priority ticket in the model-driven app, and open the run history to check every step succeeded.

A Condition would also work for High versus everything else. Switch is cleaner when there are three or more outcomes.

Common mistakes

  • Trying to add a second trigger to one flow. You need a second flow instead.
  • Assuming Dataverse is a standard connector because it is from Microsoft. It is premium.
  • Confusing a connector with a connection. The connector is the bridge; the connection is your sign-in to use it.
  • Using Apply to each when there is only one item, or forgetting it is added automatically when you use a list value.
  • Writing an expression by hand when simply picking dynamic content would do.

How the exam asks about it

  • "What starts the flow" points to the trigger. "Two events should both start the process" means two flows.
  • "Needs a premium licence" points to Dataverse, SQL Server, HTTP or custom connectors. Outlook, Teams and SharePoint are standard.
  • "For every item", "each row" point to Apply to each. "Until", "keep checking" point to Do until. "Several possible values" points to Switch.
  • "Use a value from an earlier step" points to dynamic content. "Calculate", "format" or "add days" points to an expression.

lessons.title: Build flows with AI
lessons.summaryHtml:
Cloud flows: describe the flow on the Power Automate home page, for example “When a file is added to a SharePoint folder, post a message in Teams”. Copilot proposes the trigger and actions. You confirm the connections, then refine it in the designer by chatting with Copilot (“add a condition for files over 1 MB”). Copilot can also explain a flow and help write expressions.

Desktop flows: Copilot in Power Automate for desktop can create actions or scripts from a description and answer questions about the flow.

Flows can also call AI directly, for example running an AI prompt to summarise or classify text.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

You can build flows by describing what you want in everyday language. Copilot, the AI assistant in Power Automate, turns your description into a draft flow.

Think of it like telling a skilled colleague, "Every time a file lands in this folder, tell the team in Teams." The colleague sets up the first version. You then check it, adjust it and approve it.

AI helps in two ways:

  • Building flows: Copilot creates, edits and explains flows from your words.
  • Inside flows: a flow step can call AI, for example to summarise, classify or extract information from text.

Why it matters

Beginners often know what they want but not which trigger, connector or action to choose. Copilot removes that first hurdle. It also speeds up experienced makers who would otherwise click through many menus.

Imagine a new student worker in the help desk. They know the team wants a daily summary of open tickets, but they have never built a flow. With Copilot they describe the goal, review the proposed steps and have a working draft in minutes. They still learn the structure, because they can see and edit every step Copilot adds.

How it works

1. Describe the flow. On the Power Automate home page, you type what the flow should do. A good description names the trigger, the data and the result. For example: "When a file is added to a SharePoint folder, post a message in Teams."

2. Review the proposal. Copilot suggests a trigger and actions. You read them before continuing.

3. Set up connections. Each connector in the flow needs a connection, which is a saved sign-in. Copilot lists them and you confirm existing ones or create new ones. The flow cannot run until this is done.

4. Refine in the designer. The designer has a Copilot pane. You can chat with it to change the open flow, for example "add a condition so only files over 1 MB are posted". You can also ask it questions, such as "what does this flow do?" or "why did this step fail?".

5. Test and fix. Run the flow with real or test data. Check the run history. Ask Copilot to explain errors, then fix them.

Copilot can also help write expressions. You describe the value in words and it proposes the formula for you to check.

WhereWhat Copilot can doWhat you still do
Power Automate home pageCreate a new cloud flow from a descriptionCheck the steps, confirm connections
Cloud flow designerAdd, change or remove steps; explain the flow; help with expressions and errorsDecide what is correct, test the result
Power Automate for desktopSuggest actions or scripts from a description; answer questions about the desktop flowReview, run and test on the Windows machine
Inside a flow (AI steps)Run a prompt to summarise, classify or draft text; extract data from documentsWrite clear instructions, check quality, keep a human review where needed

AI prompt steps. A flow can send text to an AI prompt and use the answer in later steps. A prompt is a set of instructions, such as "Classify this ticket as Hardware, Software or Network. Reply with one word." The result becomes dynamic content, just like any other step output.

Agent flows. In Copilot Studio, you can also build agent flows. These are fixed, step-by-step flows that an agent calls when it needs a reliable process. You will meet them again in the agents lessons.

Watch out: Copilot drafts; it does not take responsibility. It may pick the wrong column or connector. The maker must always review, set up connections and test before sharing the flow.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The team lead wants a daily email of open tickets and wants new tickets sorted into categories automatically.

  1. On the Power Automate home page, type: "Every day at 5 pm, list Dataverse tickets with status Open and email me a summary."
  2. Copilot proposes: a Recurrence trigger, a Dataverse "List rows" action on Ticket, and an Outlook "Send an email" action.
  3. Confirm the Dataverse and Outlook connections, then create the flow.
  4. In the designer’s Copilot pane, type: "Only include tickets with High priority." Copilot updates the filter. Open the step and check it filters on Priority, not on another column.
  5. Test the flow. If the email is empty, ask Copilot: "Why did the list return no rows?" and follow its suggestion.
  6. Build a second flow for new tickets. Add an AI prompt step: "Read this description and reply with Hardware, Software or Network." Use the answer to set the ticket’s Category.
  7. Add a Condition: if the AI answer is not one of the three values, send the ticket to a staff member for manual review.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a Copilot-drafted flow is ready to run. Connections must be set up and the flow must be tested.
  • Believing Copilot only works on new flows. It can also change and explain existing flows in the designer.
  • Writing vague descriptions like "help with tickets". Name the trigger, data and outcome.
  • Trusting AI output blindly. AI prompt results and document extraction can be wrong, so add checks or human review.
  • Assuming Copilot is only for cloud flows. Power Automate for desktop has Copilot help too.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Describe in natural language", "without knowing which connectors to use" points to creating the flow with Copilot.
  • "Change an existing flow by describing the change" or "explain what this flow does" points to the Copilot pane in the designer.
  • "The drafted flow will not run" or "what must you do next" points to setting up connections and testing.
  • "Summarise", "classify" or "extract" text inside an automation points to an AI step in the flow, such as running a prompt.

lessons.title: Agent use cases
lessons.summaryHtml:
Copilot Studio builds agents: AI assistants that answer questions from knowledge, hold conversations and take actions.

  • Conversational agents chat with people in Teams, on a website or in Microsoft 365 Copilot.
  • Autonomous agents start on an event, such as a new email, and work without anyone chatting.

Common use cases: IT help desk, HR policy questions, customer service, employee onboarding, sales assistance.

With generative orchestration, the agent uses AI to decide which topics, tools and knowledge to use for each message. Classic agents rely more on matching trigger phrases.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An agent is an AI assistant you build in Microsoft Copilot Studio. It can answer questions, hold a conversation and take actions for people.

Think of a new staff member at a front desk. You give them a job description (instructions). You hand them a folder of facts (knowledge). You teach them a few fixed routines (topics). You give them keys to certain systems (tools). You tell them which desk to sit at (channels). An agent is built from the same parts.

Copilot Studio is a low-code tool. You can start by describing the agent in plain language, and Copilot drafts it for you. You then review and improve it.

Why it matters

Many questions at work are repeated again and again. "How do I reset my password?" "What is the leave policy?" "Where is my order?" People wait for answers, and staff spend hours typing the same replies.

An agent can answer these questions at any time of day, in the tools people already use, such as Microsoft Teams or a website. It can also do simple jobs, like logging a request or checking a status. Staff are then free for the hard problems.

Common use cases include:

  • IT help desk: fix common problems and log tickets.
  • HR questions: answer policy questions from internal documents.
  • Customer service: answer product questions on a public website and hand over to a person when needed.
  • Employee onboarding: guide new starters through their first weeks.
  • Sales help: look up customer or product details quickly.
  • Background work: sort incoming emails or requests with nobody chatting.

How it works

The anatomy of an agent. Every agent is made of the same building blocks:

PartWhat it isFront-desk analogy
Name and descriptionSays who the agent is and what it is for.Name badge and job title
InstructionsPlain-language guidance on goals, tone and limits, for example "Be brief and friendly. Only help with campus IT."Job description
TopicsFixed conversation paths for specific tasks.Step-by-step routines
KnowledgeContent the agent answers from, such as websites, SharePoint or files.Reference folder
ToolsThings the agent can do, such as run a flow or call a connector.Keys to other systems
TriggersEvents that start an agent without a chat, such as a new email arriving.An alarm that says "start work now"
ChannelsWhere people reach the agent, such as Teams or a website.Which desk or phone line they use

Two ways agents work with people.

  • Conversational agents wait for a person to type or speak. They chat in Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, a website or other channels.
  • Autonomous agents start from a trigger, such as a new email, a new record or a schedule. They work in the background and act without anyone chatting.

One agent can be both. It might chat with students and also run when a new email arrives.

Orchestration: how the agent decides what to do. Orchestration means choosing which part of the agent should handle a message.

Generative orchestrationClassic orchestration
How it choosesAI reads the names and descriptions of topics, tools and knowledge, then picks the best fit.Matches the user's words to each topic's trigger phrases.
Multiple stepsCan combine several topics, tools and knowledge in one answer.Usually runs one topic at a time.
Missing informationAsks the user for missing tool inputs by itself.You must build Question nodes for every input.
What you writeClear descriptions and instructions.Many trigger phrases per topic.

With classic orchestration, if no topic matches, the agent can fall back to searching its knowledge for an answer. With generative orchestration, knowledge is simply one more option the AI can choose.

Remember: under generative orchestration, the description is what the AI reads to decide. A vague description leads to wrong choices.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The IT team wants a "Help Desk Assistant" for students.

  1. In Copilot Studio, the maker creates a new agent by describing it: "Helps students fix common IT problems and log help desk tickets."
  2. Copilot drafts a name, description and instructions. The maker edits the instructions: "Use short, friendly sentences. Only answer campus IT questions. Offer to log a ticket if the problem is not solved."
  3. Knowledge: the maker adds an IT FAQ document and the college's public IT web pages.
  4. Topics: a "Log a ticket" topic collects the problem and priority.
  5. Tools: a "Create ticket" agent flow adds a row to the Ticket table in Dataverse.
  6. Trigger: later, the team adds a trigger so the agent reads each new email to the help desk mailbox and creates a ticket. That part is autonomous.
  7. Channels: the agent is published to Microsoft Teams for students.

A student asks, "How do I connect to campus Wi-Fi?" Generative orchestration sees this is a knowledge question and answers from the FAQ, with a citation. Another student says, "My laptop won't charge, please log it." The agent picks the "Create ticket" tool instead.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking an agent is only a chatbot. Agents can also take actions and run on triggers with nobody chatting.
  • Confusing instructions with topics. Instructions are general guidance for every reply. Topics are fixed paths for specific tasks.
  • Writing weak descriptions. With generative orchestration, a description like "Topic 1" gives the AI nothing to choose from.
  • Believing classic agents need no maintenance. Classic agents need many trigger phrases, and they must be updated as people ask in new ways.
  • Mixing up Copilot Studio and Power Automate. Copilot Studio builds agents. Flows are tools the agent can call.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Runs when an email arrives", "no user interaction", "in the background" point to an autonomous agent with a trigger.
  • "Chat with employees in Teams" or "answer questions on the website" point to a conversational agent.
  • "AI decides which topic, tool or knowledge to use", "chain several actions" point to generative orchestration.
  • "Match trigger phrases" points to classic orchestration. "Set the tone" or "limit what the agent talks about" points to instructions.
