lessons.title: Topics: conversation paths
lessons.summaryHtml:
A topic is a conversation path for a specific task. It starts from trigger phrases or, with generative orchestration, from a description of when to use it.

Common nodes inside a topic:

  • Message: the agent says something.
  • Question: asks the user and saves the answer in a variable.
  • Condition: branches on a value.
  • Action / tool call: runs a flow, connector or other tool.
  • Redirect to another topic, and End conversation.

System topics come built in: Conversation start, Greeting, Escalate, Fallback (when the agent doesn’t understand) and others. Use topics when a conversation must follow a predictable, structured path.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A topic is a conversation path for one task. It is like a script a call-centre worker follows: greet, ask a question, check the answer, then do the next step.

You build a topic on a canvas by adding nodes. Each node is one step, such as sending a message or asking a question. The answers people give are stored in variables, which are named boxes that hold values.

Why it matters

AI answers are flexible, but some tasks must follow the same steps every time. A help desk must always capture the problem and the priority before logging a ticket. A bank must always check identity before sharing details.

Topics give you that control. You decide exactly what is asked, in what order, and what happens next. Topics also make an agent's behaviour easy to test and explain.

How it works

How a topic starts. A topic has a trigger that decides when it runs.

  • With generative orchestration, you write a description of when to use the topic, for example "Use when the user wants to report an IT problem." The AI reads it and decides.
  • With classic orchestration, you add trigger phrases, such as "log a ticket" or "report a problem". The agent matches what the user types to these phrases.
  • Some topics start from events instead, for example when a conversation starts or when an error happens.

Common nodes.

NodeWhat it doesExample
MessageThe agent says something. It can include variables."Thanks, I have your problem noted."
QuestionAsks the user and saves the answer into a variable. Can offer multiple-choice options."What's the priority?" Low, Medium, High
ConditionBranches the path based on a value.If Priority is High, go one way.
Variable managementSets or clears a variable's value.Set Status to "Open".
Call a tool or actionRuns an agent flow, connector or other tool.Run "Create ticket".
RedirectJumps to another topic.Go to "Check ticket status".
Transfer and End conversationHands over to a human, or finishes the conversation.Escalate to live staff.

Variables and their scope. Scope means where a variable can be used.

TypeWhere it worksExample
Topic variableOnly inside the topic that created it.Topic.ProblemTitle
Global variableIn every topic, for the whole conversation.Global.StudentId, asked once and reused
System variableBuilt in and filled by Copilot Studio. You read them but don't create them.System.User.DisplayName, the signed-in user's name

Topics can also pass values to each other. A topic can receive input values and return output values, so one topic can call another and use its result.

System topics. Every agent comes with built-in system topics. You can edit many of them, but you should not delete them. Examples:

  • Conversation Start: the first message when a chat opens.
  • Greeting: replies to "hi" or "hello".
  • Fallback: runs when the agent can't understand or match the request.
  • Escalate: runs when the user asks for a human.
  • End of Conversation and On Error, among others.
Remember: use a topic when the conversation must follow a predictable, structured path. Use knowledge when you just need an answer from content.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The maker builds a "Log a ticket" topic for the Help Desk Assistant.

  1. Create a topic named "Log a ticket" with the description: "Use when the user wants to report an IT problem."
  2. Add a Question node: "What's the problem?" Save the answer as the topic variable ProblemTitle.
  3. Add a multiple-choice Question: "How urgent is it?" with Low, Medium and High. Save it as Priority.
  4. Add a Condition: if Priority is High, send a Message: "I've marked this as urgent. Staff will look at it first."
  5. Add a Message that repeats the values back to the user.
  6. Edit the Greeting system topic so it also says the help desk opening hours.

A Message node can show variable values inside text:

Got it. Problem: {Topic.ProblemTitle}. Priority: {Topic.Priority}.

If the student's name is needed in many topics, the maker uses the system variable for the user's display name instead of asking for it again.

Common mistakes

  • Using a Message node to collect input. A Message only speaks. Only a Question node saves the user's answer.
  • Expecting a topic variable in another topic. Topic variables stay in their topic. Use a global variable or pass the value as an input.
  • Deleting system topics. They handle key moments like errors and fallback. Edit them instead.
  • Building a topic for every question. Simple factual questions are better answered from knowledge.
  • Too few trigger phrases in a classic agent. People phrase requests in many ways, so a topic with one phrase is often missed.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Collect", "ask for", "store the user's answer" point to a Question node.
  • "Different path depending on the answer" points to a Condition node. "Go to another topic" points to Redirect.
  • "Reuse a value across all topics in the conversation" points to a global variable. "Built-in value like the user's name" points to a system variable.
  • "When the agent doesn't understand" points to Fallback. "User asks for a human" points to Escalate.

lessons.title: Knowledge sources
lessons.summaryHtml:
Knowledge lets an agent answer questions from your content, with citations to the source.

  • Public websites.
  • SharePoint sites and OneDrive.
  • Uploaded files such as PDFs and Word documents.
  • Dataverse tables.
  • Enterprise systems through connectors.

You can turn off the model’s general knowledge so answers come only from your approved sources. Internal sources need user authentication so people only see content they’re allowed to see. Keep sources accurate: the agent can only be as good as its content.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Knowledge is the content an agent reads to answer questions. It can be a website, a SharePoint site, uploaded files or data in Dataverse.

Imagine a librarian. They don't memorise every book. When you ask a question, they look it up in the right book and show you the page. A knowledge-based agent does the same. It finds the relevant content, writes an answer and adds a citation, a link to where the answer came from.

Why it matters

Organisations already have lots of useful content: FAQs, policy documents, product manuals and web pages. Writing a topic for every question in them would take forever.

With knowledge, you point the agent at the content and it can answer many questions at once. When the document changes, answers change too. Citations let people check the source, which builds trust.

How it works

Types of knowledge sources.

SourceGood forNotes
Public websiteContent anyone can read, like a college website.No sign-in needed.
SharePoint and OneDriveInternal documents such as HR policies.Users must sign in. They only get answers from content they are allowed to see.
Uploaded filesA few specific documents, such as a PDF or Word FAQ.Stored with the agent. Upload again when the file changes.
Dataverse tablesBusiness data, such as tickets or products.Answers questions about records in your tables.
Enterprise systems via connectorsContent in other business systems.Brings in data from outside Microsoft 365.

How an answer is produced.

  1. The user asks a question.
  2. The agent searches its knowledge sources for relevant passages.
  3. The AI writes an answer based on those passages. This is called a grounded answer, because it is based on real content.
  4. The agent shows the answer with citations.

General knowledge. The AI model also has its own broad knowledge of the world. You can switch this off. Then the agent only answers from your approved sources. If they don't cover the question, the agent says it can't help, or falls back to another path.

Knowledge or topics?

NeedUse
Answer many factual questions from existing documentsKnowledge
Follow fixed steps, collect details, then actTopic
Always give the exact same wording, for example a legal statementTopic with a Message node
Content changes often and lives in SharePointKnowledge

Most real agents use both. Knowledge handles the broad questions. Topics handle the structured tasks.

Watch out: the agent is only as good as its content. Old, wrong or conflicting documents lead to old, wrong or conflicting answers.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The Help Desk Assistant needs to answer common IT questions.

  1. The maker writes a one-page "IT FAQ" covering Wi-Fi, printing and password reset, and uploads it as knowledge.
  2. They add the college's public IT web pages as a second source.
  3. Staff procedures are kept on an internal SharePoint site. The maker adds it too, so signed-in staff can ask about them. Students without access to that site won't get answers from it.
  4. They switch off general knowledge, so the agent never guesses about campus rules.
  5. Testing: "How do I print from my laptop?" The agent answers from the FAQ, with a citation to it.
  6. Testing: "Who won the football match yesterday?" The sources don't cover this, so the agent says it can only help with campus IT.

For logging a ticket, the maker still uses the "Log a ticket" topic, because that needs fixed steps and an action.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking knowledge trains the AI model. It doesn't. The agent searches your content at the time of each question.
  • Adding internal content without sign-in. Internal sources like SharePoint need user authentication so people see only what they are allowed to.
  • Leaving general knowledge on when answers must be strictly from company content. Switch it off.
  • Using knowledge for a process. Knowledge answers questions. It doesn't ask questions in order or create records.
  • Uploading a file and forgetting it. An uploaded copy doesn't update itself when the original changes.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Answer from internal documents", "HR policies in SharePoint" point to SharePoint as a knowledge source.
  • "Only from approved sources", "don't make things up" point to switching off general knowledge.
  • "Show where the answer came from" points to citations from knowledge.
  • "Structured steps" or "collect details then act" means a topic, not knowledge.

lessons.title: Tools: agent flows, connectors and MCP
lessons.summaryHtml:
Tools let an agent do things, not just talk.

  • Agent flows: automations built in Copilot Studio. They run their steps exactly as designed every time, which suits tasks like creating a record.
  • Connector actions: the same connectors as Power Automate.
  • Prompts: reusable AI prompts.
  • REST APIs and custom connectors for your own services.
  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers: an open standard for plugging external tools and data into agents. Add a server and the agent gets all of its tools, which stay up to date as the server changes.

The agent decides when to call a tool from the tool’s name and description, and asks the user for any missing inputs. Clear descriptions matter.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Tools let an agent do things, not just talk. With tools, an agent can create a record, send an email, look up an order or call another system.

Think of a hotel receptionist. Answering questions is useful. But the receptionist becomes really helpful when they can also book a room, order a taxi or print a bill. Those abilities are the receptionist's tools.

Why it matters

A student who reports a broken laptop doesn't just want advice. They want a ticket logged. Without tools, the agent can only say "please fill in the form". With a tool, the agent logs the ticket itself during the chat.

Tools turn an agent from an information desk into a real assistant that finishes tasks. They also let the agent fetch live data, like a ticket's current status, instead of old copies.

How it works

Tool types.

Tool typeWhat it isWhen to use it
Agent flowA flow built in Copilot Studio. It runs its steps exactly as designed every time.Tasks that must be predictable, such as creating a Dataverse row or approvals.
Connector actionOne action from the same connectors Power Automate uses, such as Outlook or SharePoint.A single quick action in a common service.
PromptA reusable AI prompt with inputs, for example "summarise this text".AI tasks like summarising, classifying or drafting.
REST API or custom connectorA connection to your own web service.Your organisation's own systems that have an API.
MCP serverA server using the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for sharing tools and data with agents.Plugging in a set of external tools that stay in sync with the server.

Agent flows. An agent flow is deterministic. That means the same input always follows the same steps. The AI decides when to call it, but the flow decides how the work is done. This is ideal for business rules that must not change.

MCP. When you add an MCP server, the agent gets all the tools that server offers. If the server owner adds or changes a tool, the agent sees the change automatically. You don't rebuild anything.

How the agent picks a tool. With generative orchestration, the agent reads each tool's name and description. It compares them with what the user asked and chooses the best match.

  1. The user says what they want.
  2. The agent compares the request with tool, topic and knowledge descriptions.
  3. It picks a tool and looks at the tool's inputs.
  4. It fills inputs from the conversation. If something is missing, it asks the user.
  5. It runs the tool and uses the outputs in its reply.

Inputs and outputs can have descriptions too. A good input description, such as "Priority of the ticket: Low, Medium or High", helps the agent fill it correctly.

Remember: the description is the tool's instruction label. "Creates a help desk ticket when a student reports a problem" works. "Flow 2" does not.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The maker adds a "Create ticket" tool to the Help Desk Assistant.

  1. In the agent, add a tool and choose a new agent flow named "Create ticket".
  2. Give the flow two inputs: Title (text) and Priority (text).
  3. Add the Dataverse action "Add a new row" to the Ticket table. Map Title and Priority. Set Status to Open.
  4. End the flow by responding to the agent with the new ticket's ID.
  5. Write the tool description: "Creates a help desk ticket when a student reports a problem."
  6. Test: "My laptop won't charge and it's urgent."

The agent recognises a problem report and picks "Create ticket". It fills Title from the message. It reads "urgent" and may set Priority to High, or ask to confirm. The flow runs and the agent replies: "Your ticket is logged. Your ticket ID is ..." The maker then checks the Ticket table and sees the new row.

Later, the maker adds a connector action to send a Teams message to staff for every High-priority ticket.

Common mistakes

  • Using knowledge to take actions. Knowledge only answers. Creating or changing data needs a tool.
  • Vague tool names and descriptions. The agent can't choose a tool it can't understand.
  • Thinking the AI runs agent flow steps its own way. The AI chooses to call the flow. The steps inside always run as designed.
  • Thinking MCP is a Microsoft-only product. It is an open standard used across many AI tools.
  • Forgetting connections. Connector-based tools need a working connection before they can run.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Same way every time", "reliable", "create a record" point to an agent flow.
  • "Open standard", "external tools stay in sync" point to an MCP server.
  • "Summarise or classify text with AI as a step" points to a prompt tool.
  • "Agent calls the wrong tool" or "never calls it" points to improving the tool's name and description.

terms.definition: Something an agent can call to take an action or fetch data.
A deterministic flow an agent can run.
Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting agents to tools and data.

Back in the agent, add the flow as a tool and set its description to the text in the file.

Test 2 makes the agent ask how urgent the problem is before calling the tool.

lessons.title: Publish to channels
lessons.summaryHtml:
Publishing makes the latest version of your agent live. Changes don’t reach users until you publish again.

After publishing, you make the agent available on channels:

  • Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot.
  • A demo website for quick testing.
  • Your own website, using embed code.
  • Mobile apps, SharePoint and other channels through Azure Bot Service.

The agent’s authentication setting affects which channels are available. For example, Teams and Microsoft 365 use Microsoft sign-in.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Publishing makes the latest version of your agent live. Channels are the places where people talk to it, such as Microsoft Teams or a website.

Think of a shop. Stocking new products in the back room is like editing the agent. Putting them on the shelves is publishing. The shop's branches are the channels. Until you put things on the shelves, customers can't see them, no matter how many branches you have.

Why it matters

An agent that nobody can reach is useless. People also want help where they already work. Staff live in Teams. Customers visit the website. Some users work inside Microsoft 365 Copilot.

Publishing also protects users from half-finished work. You can edit and test freely. Users only see changes when you decide they are ready.

How it works

Publishing.

  • You edit and test the agent in Copilot Studio's test pane.
  • When ready, you select Publish. The current version becomes the live one.
  • Every later change needs another publish before users see it.
  • One publish updates the agent on all its channels.

Common channels.

ChannelWho uses itNotes
Microsoft Teams and Microsoft 365 CopilotEmployees and staffUses Microsoft sign-in. An admin may need to approve it for the whole organisation.
Demo websiteTesters and reviewersA ready-made test page to share for quick feedback. Not for production.
Custom websitePublic visitors or customersCopilot Studio gives embed code to paste into your own web page.
SharePointEmployees on an intranet sitePuts the agent on internal pages.
Mobile apps and other channelsApp users and other platformsSome use Azure Bot Service to connect.

Authentication options. Authentication decides whether users must sign in, and it affects which channels and sources work. At a general level there are three choices:

OptionWhat it meansTypical fit
No authenticationAnyone who can reach the agent can chat. The agent doesn't know who they are.A public website answering public questions.
Authenticate with MicrosoftUsers sign in with their Microsoft work account through Microsoft Entra ID.Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot and SharePoint for staff.
Authenticate manuallyThe maker sets up a sign-in provider themselves.Custom websites or apps that need a sign-in.

Sign-in matters for more than security. Internal knowledge, like SharePoint, needs to know who the user is, so each person only gets answers from content they may see. Tools that act on a user's behalf need this too.

Watch out: if the agent has no authentication, internal sources and Microsoft sign-in channels won't work as expected.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The Help Desk Assistant is tested and ready.

  1. The maker checks the authentication setting is Microsoft sign-in, because students and staff have college Microsoft accounts.
  2. They select Publish.
  3. They open the demo website channel and send the link to two classmates for quick feedback.
  4. They add the agent to Microsoft Teams. The IT admin approves it so all students can find it.
  5. Later, they change the Greeting message to show new opening hours. Teams still shows the old greeting.
  6. They publish again. Now Teams shows the new greeting.

The college also wants a small public agent on its open website for visitors. Because visitors have no college account, that agent uses no authentication and answers only from public web pages. It is added with embed code from the custom website channel.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting edits to go live on save. Users only see changes after you publish.
  • Using the demo website for real customers. It's for testing. Use the custom website channel for your own site.
  • Mixing up publish and channels. Publishing makes a version live. Channels decide where users reach it.
  • Choosing no authentication for internal content. Internal sources need signed-in users.
  • Thinking you must publish each channel separately. One publish updates the agent everywhere it is connected.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Changes don't appear", "users still see the old answer" point to publishing again.
  • "Put the agent on our own website" points to the custom website channel and embed code.
  • "Quick link for testers" points to the demo website.
  • "Staff sign in with work accounts in Teams" points to Microsoft authentication. "Anonymous public visitors" points to no authentication.

lessons.title: Manage agents: analytics, evaluations and Agent 365
lessons.summaryHtml:
Once agents are live, you monitor and improve them.

  • Analytics in Copilot Studio: sessions, engagement, resolution and escalation rates, abandoned conversations, satisfaction scores, and which topics and knowledge get used. Transcripts help you see real conversations.
  • Adoption: track how many people use agents over time and where usage grows or drops.
  • Agent evaluations: build test sets of questions with expected answers or criteria, run them automatically, and rerun after each change to catch regressions.
  • Microsoft Agent 365: a control plane for IT to manage every agent in the organisation, wherever it was built. It covers an inventory of agents, access and identity, visibility into what agents do, and security and compliance.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Building an agent is only the start. Once it's live, you need to know if it helps people, test that it stays good, and keep all agents safe and under control.

Think of running a restaurant. Analytics are your sales and customer feedback reports. Evaluations are taste tests before a new menu goes out. Microsoft Agent 365 is the head office that knows every branch, who works there, and whether each follows the rules.

Why it matters

An agent can quietly fail. People may give up halfway, or get wrong answers after someone edits a document. Without data, nobody notices until complaints arrive.

Organisations also end up with many agents, built by different teams and tools. IT must know which agents exist, what data they can reach, and whether they are secure. Without a central view, that is almost impossible.

How it works

Analytics in Copilot Studio. Each agent has analytics that summarise its conversations over time.

MetricWhat it tells youWhat to do if it looks bad
SessionsHow many conversations happened.Low use may mean people don't know about the agent.
Engagement rateShare of sessions where the user actually got into a topic or task.Improve greeting, descriptions or knowledge.
Resolution rateShare of sessions the agent resolved without a human.Add content or topics for common problems.
Escalation rateShare of sessions handed over to a person.Find what the agent can't handle yet.
Abandon rateShare of sessions where users left before finishing.Shorten long topics or fix confusing questions.
Satisfaction (CSAT)How users rated their experience.Read low-scoring conversations to find causes.
Topic and knowledge usageWhich topics and sources get used most, and questions left unanswered.Focus improvements where the traffic is.

Transcripts let you read real conversations, which shows why a number looks the way it does. Adoption views show how many people use agents over time and where use grows or drops.

Agent evaluations. An evaluation is an automated test for your agent.

  1. You create a test set: questions plus the expected answers, or criteria a good answer should meet.
  2. You run it. The agent answers every question automatically.
  3. Each answer is scored against what you expected.
  4. After any change, you run the same test set again. If scores drop, you have a regression, meaning something that used to work is now broken.

Evaluations replace slow manual testing, where someone types the same questions by hand after every change.

Microsoft Agent 365. Agent 365 is a control plane for IT. A control plane is one central place to manage many things. It covers all agents in the organisation, wherever they were built, not just Copilot Studio agents.

  • Inventory or registry: one list of every agent.
  • Access and identity: control which agents can reach which people, data and systems.
  • Visibility: see what agents are doing and how they are used.
  • Security and compliance: protect against threats and keep data handling within company rules.
NeedFeature
How is my one agent performing with real users?Analytics
Did my change break answer quality?Evaluations
What agents exist across the company, and are they secure?Agent 365

Example: Campus Help Desk

The Help Desk Assistant has been live in Teams for a month.

  1. The maker opens Analytics. "Log a ticket" is the most used topic. Many questions about exam printing went unanswered.
  2. The abandon rate is high in "Log a ticket". Transcripts show students quit when asked for a long description.
  3. The maker creates an evaluation with questions from the IT FAQ, such as "How do I reset my password?", each with the expected answer. The first run gives a baseline score.
  4. They add an exam printing section to the FAQ and shorten the ticket questions. Then they publish.
  5. They run the evaluation again. Scores stay high, so nothing broke. Next month, analytics show fewer abandoned sessions.
  6. Meanwhile, the college IT team uses Agent 365 to see every agent across campus, including the Help Desk Assistant, and checks which data each one can reach.

Common mistakes

  • Treating a high session count as success. Many sessions with low resolution means many unhappy users.
  • Testing by hand only once. Every change can break something. Rerun evaluations after changes.
  • Thinking Agent 365 builds agents. It manages and governs them. Agents are built in tools like Copilot Studio.
  • Thinking Agent 365 only covers Copilot Studio. It is meant for agents across the organisation, wherever built.
  • Ignoring transcripts. Numbers show that something is wrong. Transcripts show why.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Share of conversations handled without a human" points to resolution rate. "Users leave before finishing" points to abandon rate.
  • "Automatically test answer quality", "catch regressions", "rerun after changes" point to agent evaluations.
  • "One inventory of all agents", "govern and secure agents across the organisation" point to Microsoft Agent 365.
  • "See what users actually said" points to conversation transcripts.
